summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 on the net wealth of the assessee. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 as the net assets of the appellant assessee. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa) (1), and held that the net value of the net asset of the respondent was Rs. 2,00000 as against the net income of the other assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court erred in holding that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the asses see. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the value of an assessee called upon to pay a certain sum of money by way of net wealth is not permissible under section 27 of the Wealth Tax Act. [309F] 2. The net wealth must be determined according to the provisions of the Income Tax Act as the estimated price, which in the opinion of the wealth Tax Officer the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valuation date. It is apparent from the definition or "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value". [309G] 3. The concept or "corporate debtor" has to be understood in a broad sense and it cannot be interpreted in a narrow sense as to include a person who is not an assessee within the meaning of the Act. It must be remembered that the expression "net assets" which refers to "the total value". In the context of the definition, the word "creditor" has been used in the context in which it occurs and it is not possible to say that the word 'corporate creditor ' has been defined in the Income tax Act. The definition or the "net asset" which mentions "the amount of all the assets" belonging to the assessee on the date of the assessment year, does not mean that the value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimate date. [310H; 311A B] 4. In the instant case, the net valuation date is not the actual date of receipt of the amount by the assessee but the outstandings of the money lending business are liable to tax under the Wealth tax Act, and that is why the method of accounting, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for determining the assets of an assesses. [311C D] 5. The expression "cable value" in section 2(1) (a) of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1962 means the last day of the previous year as defined under the Income 'tax Act. In this view of the matter, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesses are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, though not realised, on the out standings of money lending and other financial or hydrina Narasimha Rao (Orissa), (Orissa). (ii) The computation made by the Wealth ' Tax Officer is correct.

The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground of defi cation that he had been convicted by a criminal court for misconduct. The Tribunal held that the respondent had committed an offence under section 3(1)(d) of the . He was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal could not have exercised its power of judicial review over the order of dismissal passed by a competent authority on a public servant, if the disciplinary authority had taken into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case, and that the tribunal could exercise such powers only if the charge proved alone would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal is based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. [27D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent did not have any material before the Tribunal to justify his action. The tribunal could not sit as a court of appeal over a decision based on it. If the conclusion that the inquiry officer was not in fact the person convicted, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would weigh with the Authority in dismissing him. [28F] 1:3. In the case of proceedings transfer from one civil court or High Court to another civil court, the Tribunal has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers which are exercisable by a court under the . [29G H] 1 4. The Supreme Court has no power to interfere in an appeal over the decision of a competent tribunal on a finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it has not been shown that there had been violation of the rules of natural justice. If it is his case that he was not a party to the proceedings, he cannot be heard to say that the charge established alone would not have weighed in favour of the authority. [29H] 1 5. The High Court could not exercise its power under Article 226 over a matter which has been referred to it by the Tribunal. If there had already been any violation of rules of Natural Justice, the order cannot be interfered with. [30A B] State of Orissa vs Tulsiram Patel, ; , followed.

The appellants were the legal representatives of a deceased plaintiff in a suit filed by the respondent. The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the property in question on the ground that the appellant was not a tenant and that he had been evicted from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao '. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff was not entitled to be a deemed purchaser of the land in respect of which he claimed to be lessee. The first appellate court also held that the suit was barred by Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In second appeal, the High Court held that since the respondent had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession under section 18 of the Act and had therefore filed a fresh suit, the subsequent suit was not maintainable. The appellants preferred an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil court is specifically barred by sub section (2) of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the Mamlatdar. [32F] 1.2 In view of the fact that the respondent was sued as a trespasser raising a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of lease can be decided by the Civil Court as incidental to the grant of relief for possession or is the Civil court precluded from deciding the same in view of section 7 read Section 58(2) which provides that if in any suit instituted in a civil court issues which are required to he settled, decide and dealt with under the statute, the jurisdiction of Civil Courts stands wholly barred by virtue of Section58(2). [32G H] 1:3. The jurisdiction is vested in the Mamlatdar under section 7 of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1939. If on the other hand, the Mamlatdar rejects the plea raised under the Tenancy Act the Civil Courts would be entitled to deal with the dispute on the footing that the defendant is a trespasser. [33H; 34A] 1.:4. The question whether defendant No.1 was a tenant in respect o the land or not should be referred to the civil Court for decision and after his decision is received by the civil courts if the issue is held against defendant No 1, the Civil Judge would be required to follow the course that may be found appropriate in the fact situation arising out of the pleadings in this case and the nature of the questions required to determine for grant or refusal of relief claimed in the suit. [34D E] 1 :5. The High Court has not committed any error in holding that defendant No1 was not an 'tenant ' within the meaning of section 58(1) of Act. [35F G] 1 Whether defendant No,1 proved that he was a trespasser and whether his claim of tenancy can be adjudicated by the Revenue Court as ancillary to the granting of relief under section 8(2), is a question which falls within the ambit of section 57(2)(a) of Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act. The Civil Court would not be competent to pass any order for restoration of possession to the deemed tenant. [36F G; 37A] 2:1.

The petitioners are working as daily rated employees. They have been paid the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The Corporation has also fixed the minimum wage payable to them. The petitioners claim payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. The State Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable to the petitioners engaged in the construction industry. They are being paid the same wages as were payable to carpenters, painters and carpent workers employed in the Construction industry. The Court directed the Central Government to fix the pay scale of the petitioner on par with his counterparts doing similar work under the same employer. In the meantime, the Corporation has made an application for fixation of the minimum pay scale for similar work in the building industry. This application was rejected by the State Government on the ground that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act. The petitioner has filed this writ petition challenging the order of the State Govern ment as well as the Central Govern ment. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of equal pay for equal work cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It is important to emphasize that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done it cannot be judged by the mere volume of work there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. It has not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected. [667C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners are claiming wages payable for the work performed by them in Government service. They cannot enforce the right to "equal pay for Equal work". unless it is shown that there was a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment.

The prosecution case against the accused 1 to 4 was that on 29.11.1975 at Babultara and Waghala villages, all the seven accused were found in possession of a gun and a pistol. The first accused was also found guilty of the offence under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted them on the ground that they had not been charged for conspiracy and that they were not guilty of charge No. 3 framed against them in respect of murder of Malan and convicted them under section 201 read with Section 120B I. P.C., and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The State filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the appeal and acquitted all the accused except accused 1, 6 and 7. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the prosecution had failed to prove that they committed the murder of the deceased and that the conviction of the accused under section 304 read with s 34 I P.P., could not be sustained. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not have been relied upon against him in view of the fact that he was not a party to charge No 4 which was framed only against accused 1 and 6 and that he had been rightly convicted and sentenced by the trial court under section302 read with sections 120B, I.p.C.. [707D] 2.1 The retracted Judicial confession of the appellant could not therefore be relied upon as a ground for enhancement of sentence. [708E] 2:2 In view of this fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High court of the charge of conspiracy under section 120B read with S.120B I, P. C., and accused 1 was not charged for the offence of murder punishable under section 34 read with sec. 120B IPC, it could not he relied upon to convict him under section 3(1)(a) of the Act in view Of the fact, that accused 5 was not party to the conspiracy. [808F G] 2 2:3 The retracted confession of Accused 1 and 4 could not, therefore, be relied on against him. [909G H] 2 4.

The appellant executed a will in favour of his wife, the respondent. The testator died on August 22, 1945 and the appellant was not competent to make a will. The will was registered by the Sub Registrar on July 13, 1946. On the death of the testator the appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties which were the subject matter of the will. In the plaint it was stated that the testator had executed a Will in favour Of his wife and that he had signed the same as he dictated the contents of the Will. The trial court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma and that the appellant had failed to prove its execution. On appeal, the High Court held that it was not shown that the testatrix had executed the will in question and that she understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before her put the attesting signature. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in coming to the conclusion that it is not proved that the execution of the document was signed by the testator. [445 B] (ii) The evidence of the appellant himself was considered by the trial court and his conclusion was based on the evidence adduced by him on the question of execution of a will which he had put in his presence before the testator and he understood the terms of the disposition before he put the signature to the document. [441 C] (iii) The finding of the High court that the Will was not duly executed is correct. It is true that the evidence of a witness who has signed the will does not necessarily support the appellant 's case about previous instruction because, according to him, the testatrix said that she would agree to what the appellant would get written. But this evidence cannot be used as a piece of evidence to prove the execution and attestation of the deed. [442 C] The High court was right on the finding that it had not been proved that there was an intention to execute the will by her. It was also wrong in coming into the conclusion, that the document did not contain any signature of the testatrix on the instrument when she put her signatures. [443 D E] (iv) The appellant ' s case was not established beyond reasonable doubt and he had failed in his attempt to prove that the attesting witness had signed it before he putting the attesting signatures. The High Courts were wrong in holding that the onus was heavy on the appellant to remove the suspicions surrounding the execution.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arcotors, a motor carbons and other equipment. The appellant company had been manufacturing Arcots for use as an aid or addition. The goods were sold to various persons who used to purchase the same from the appellant company. The sales tax authorities held that the goods fell under entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 and that they fall under Entry No. 41 of the second schedule to the Act. The High Court allowed the writ petition filed by the appellant holding that the appellant was not entitled to adduce evidence in support of its case. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sales tax Appellate Tribunal had wrongly held that they fell under Entry 4 of Schedule 1 of the Act and that the High Court erred in allowing the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The word "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. It will be noticed that the entry No 4 occurs in a schedule in which description of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. The first entry in the Schedule relates to "motor vehicles". The second entry is used, in the same sense as the word "electrical goods", and the third entry is not intended to cover goods sold for agricultural purposes merely because some of them are also sold to agriculturists for agricultural purpose. [562 E F] (2) The expression "accessory" is defined in the Act in which the words "requirements or accessories" are used. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as "cinema" in the market. This is evident from the entry itself considered in the context in which it occurs. [563 E] (3) The term "accessability" is not used in any particular kind of instrument or apparatus, but in the sense of a description of the goods to which they are generally put. It is used for equipment and accessories connected therewith.

The petitioners, who were the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, filed petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the Act and the rules. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered by the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad; that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was being treated to be part of a consolidated fund for the purpose of implementing the policy of the Government under which the Rules were framed. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the Act was passed for devel opment of minerals and since there was no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso to rule 21, the impugned notifications were bad. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the levy of royalty in the State of Gujarat was not in contravention with clause (a) of article 304 of Constitution inasmuch it was not being treated by the State Government as a whole and therefore the levy could not be said to be bad; and that the provisions of the impugned Act were ultra vires. Dismissing the petitions, HELD: 1. The Act is passed for public interest and the levy is in contravention thereof. [408B] 2.1 The Act does no authorise the State Govern ment to show any concession while promulgating the Rules which are in the nature of subordi nate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to confer on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purpose of implementation of the policy or rules under which it is made. [416C D] 2:2 The Act was enacted for de posession of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in public interest, levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said tax should be used only for development of minerals. [414D] 2(a) The Act has been passed for denovo consideration of the mineral rights and as such it cannot be said that there is no reasonable basis for making a classification between the area in respect of which a Parwana could be issued and the duration of the Parwana right and as also stated that the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to weaker sections of society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot he said that the same cannot be used for any other purpose. [413D E] 2 (b). The Act, therefore, does not authorise the Government to show such concession while promulgated by the legislature. [411E F] 3(a). The State Government is empowered to make rules for regulating the grant of quarry leases and the conditions subject to which royalty may be levied in that behalf. The Rules are made under section 15 of the Gujarat Mineral (Concession) Rules 1966. The rule also provides that no quarry lease shall be granted for an area exceeding 10 hectares in case of specified minor mineral and 20 hec ties in the case of other minerals. So a comparison of the relevant rules would show that a larger restriction is imposed both on the area as well as land covered by a mining lease. [409E F; 409A B] 3 (b)(i) The State Legislature has power to make laws for regulating grant of quarrying leases and also to regulate the conditions of such leases. The State cannot be permitted to impose any restrictions in the matter of payment of royalty or the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and the Rules. [ 409D E; 409E] 4(c) The word 'minerals ' is not defined in the Act. It has been used in the context of the provisions contained in the various statutes.

The appellant was the trustee of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the succession is governed by custom or usage of the particular institution and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within that meaning. HELD: (i) The appointment of trusteeship in the present case was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. [435 B] (ii) The word "regulated" in section 6 (9) is identical in both the Acts. The expression "regulated by usage" in Section 6(8) must be construed along with the phrase "succession to this office" and when so construed that part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. [427 C D] (iii) The expression 'regulated by custom ' in section 3(9)(2) must mean not hereditary but a hereditary right or because succession to that office is specifically provided for by the founder himself who created the endowment. In the present cases, the appellant had taken the matter in appeal to the Madras High Court and the High Court was wrong in holding that the appointment of the trusteeship was hereditary.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The High Court acquitted him of the charge under section 304 Part I IPC but convicted him under section 324/34 IPC and sentencing him to life imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the prosecution had failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt; (ii) the testimony of PW 4 in the first information report was not corroborated by the medical evidence; (iii) the High Court erred in convicting the accused on the sole testimony of a single witness. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of PW4 is not reliable and trustworthy. It is not possible to adopt that course in this case where the testimony is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the place of occurrence already when he arrived. It was also conceivable that those persons who arrived at the scene a little later than PW 4, did not see the assailants who might have escaped. It also stands to reason that those people who arrived after the assault were not asked PW4, who arrived on the same boat with the appellant. [707E F] 2. The fact that the witness has stated in the second information report that the deceased chased the accused as the latter was running away after the attack is true. It may be possible that those members of the assailants when he came running to the place a little earlier than PW4 did not find the assailants, who might had already escaped. [077E F; 707A] 3. The mere fact that PW 4 has stated that the accused chased the deceased as the former was running from behind the place where he fell dead would not make him any other person to be a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the assailants at all. It cannot, therefore, be said that the High court in this country is justified in convicting and sentencing the accused facing a murder charge. [607E] 4. The prosecution has failed to establish the quality of the testimony by the sole eye witness. There is no evidence on record to show that PW4 was present at the time of occurrence. It would be difficult to appreciate how he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. [808F] 5. The first information statement was not reliable as it was not supported by the contents of the FIR. The second information was not a very important piece of evidence because the witness might not have been persuaded to substitute PW 4 who arrived there at the spot a little subsequently than PW 1, 2 and 3.

The respondent assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the Income tax Officer under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount received by the deceased was not liable to be taxed as his income in the assessment year and therefore he was not entitled to assess the total income of the deceased person as if the legal representatives were the assessees. On appeal, the Tribunal held that on a correct interpretation of section 24 B the amounts which were received by a heirs and legal representatives of the assessee after his death should be deemed by fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by them if death had not occurred. The High Court, however, held that as the deceased died before the publication of the notice under section 22(2), the amounts received by him were liable to tax under section 24A (1). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that on the correct interpretation, section 24 had no application and that the words "or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died" meant that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received before his death or by his heirs and Legal representatives after his deceased death, they are liable for payment of the tax just as the legal representative of a deceased person is entitled to be assessed to tax. HELD : (i) The words "and any tax" in sub sections 1, 2 and 3 of section24B contemplate that the heirs andlegal representatives of a dead person are liable to pay income tax out of their estate. [707 B] (ii) The language used in sub s. (1), (2) and (3) of section 23 contemplates that the legal personality of a person is extended for the duration of the entire previous year in the course of which he died and therefore the income received before the death or his heirs, legal representatives after their death but in that previous year becomes assessable to income Tax in the relevant assessment year. [807 C] (iii) The expression "or other legal representative" in section 24(B) contemplates that a person was served with a notice under sub s.(2) of s 22 and no return was made within the period specified and he died before his life or by the heirs after his retirement. [608 D E] (iv) The word "or" in the context means "to be a legal representative". In the present case, the expression "and other legal representatives" has been used in section 23(1). It is not necessary that the word "and" should be interpreted in its ordinary sense.

The Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 were framed by the State Government under section 3 of the . The rules made by the Central Government under the Act were published in the Gazette on January 19, 1969. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said rules and the validity thereof on the ground that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court held that the impugned rules were ultra vires the Constitution as it was violative of articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power conferred by section 3 is not a legislative power but an executive power. It is not open to the Legislature to make any law which prescribes any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to employment or appointment to an office under the Government of India or any local or other authority within its territory. [912 D] (ii) The words "any requirement" and "any provision" in article 14 are wide enough to include a law made by Parliament but not a law enacted by it. The word "under the Government" is used in the sense of conferring a power on Parliament but is denied to the Legislatures of the States, notwithstanding anything in the Constitution, and under (b) any law in force immediately before the commencement of the Act in respect of the matter shall subject to the terms thereof and subject to such adaptations that may be made under article 372 is to continue in force until altered or repealed or amended by Parliament. [1212 D E] (iii) The word 'under the State ' in section 3(3) of the Public Employment Act, 1957, means a whole State as the venue for residential qualification and it is not denied that the words "other than the State" in section 2(2)(a) are wide. [1312 D F] (iv) The expression "any condition" in the definition of "State" in Article 12 of the Consti tution is used to mean a condition of employment within that state or Union Territory, and not a condition which is expressly mentioned in the Act.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court accepted the evidence of the prosecution with regard to the fact of seizure and that being a question to be decided only by the court of fact, this Court would not re examine the evidence for satisfying itself as to the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions reached by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from an almirah in the house in which the appellant lives, the mere fact that they were found in the almirah which is said to have been in his exclusive possession would not be sufficient to sustain the conclusion that he had secreted the letter just because it was found in his almirah which was said to be in his possession. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of the accused. [426 B] (ii) The fact that an officer of the post office having in the course of his duties access to postal articles kept or lying in the post offices, the legislature has deliberately enlarged the scope of section 52 so as to include secretion, destruction or throwing away of postal articles by an officer or a person competent to deal in the way of secreting, destroying or throwing out of postal article by an Officer of the Post Office even though they may not have been entrusted to him or even though the are riot articles with which he is required or is competent to dealt in the manner laid down by section 55. [413 C D] (iii) The mere fact of search and seizure made by the appellant does not make it a case of theft. It has not been found that he committed any theft. [414 E F] (iv) The possession of these articles was not in the possession of an officer. If on the basis of this reason alone the High court could have held that though the locked almirah contained a large number of articles belonging to the appellant, it must be deemed to be inside the possession.

The appellant was the Sarpanch of a Panchayat in the District. The respondent filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the S.D.M., dated November 28, 1963 and on the same day the High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayat. On December 25, 1963 the appellant moved an application for stay of proceedings pending before the MISC. Magistrate, Lucknow, against the respondent. The application was dismissed by the Sessions Judge on March 29, 1964. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High court had no jurisdiction to entertain the petition and that the order passed by the SDC was not a judicial order within the meaning of article 227. HELD : (i) The High Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It was not proved on the evidence that any such application was made before the Tribu nal. [1192 B] (ii) The order sheet dated December 25 1963, shows that the appellant had asked for a copy of the telegram and the telegram of his counsel in the High Courts. The High court did not consider this as an affidavit filed by the respondent on the record. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court. [1203 C] (iii) The appellant was not aware of the order dated December 21, 1963 passed by SDC. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It could not therefore be said to have committed contempt.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, Etawah. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the accused. HELD : (i) The High court erred in rejecting the statement of Ujagar Singh about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. [209 B] (ii) The extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court was admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act, and the evidence of the appellant could not be rejected merely because the mere possession of a sword so stained with human blood at the time. The evidence of this witness was corroborated by the fact that he did not know the place where the sword was recovered from the house of the accused and that he was told about it by the police officer at the Police Station on the night of the murder. [205 C D] (iii) The statement made by the deceased at the police station was inadmissible under section 24 of the Indian Evidence Act. The fact that the accused had a bath in the Canal at that hour, did not lead to any improbability in his conduct as it was corroborated in the facts and circumstances of the case. [207 D] In the present case, the evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the testimony of the two witnesses who were interested in the success of the prosecution case. The presence of the three witnesses at the place of occurrence was not very much doubtful. The statement of the deceased was supported by Paley Singh, P.W. 2, who stated that he knew the accused as a result of which he had gone to the Police station and lodged the report. It was not possible for him to have made a statement that he could have made the statement at the hospital. The mere possession or possession of the sword so weapon did not amount to a voluntary confession of offence by him. [208 E G] (iv) The evidence led in this case consisted of interested witnesses and there was no reason why the High court should not have rejected the statement. It is true that the High Courts erred in accepting the statement made at the Paleya Singh 's place, but it would be wrong to say that the statement was inadmissible as its value had been corroborated by Padey Singh. The statements of the witnesses were supported by the facts that the appellant had a sleeping in his field and he had also deposed that the deceased had gone out of the canal at that time. It could not have been possible for the appellant to make a statement which was not admissible under Section 32 of Evidence Act in evidence. [210 D E] (v) The fact of the confession made by Pamey Singh is supported by a certificate issued by him from the Police Officer, who had recorded it. The certificate given by him is conclusive and conclusive as regards the guilt of the person who has committed the murder of the victim. It cannot be said that the evidence relied on for the purpose of proving the guilt is admissible in evidence under section 33 of the Act.

The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the election. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Collector, Raipur had called upon the petitioners to file their claim for inclusion in the electoral rolls and they were informed that the nominations could be filed on or after November 25, 1978. [493C] 2.1 The High Courts have been consistently taking the view that the Collector, Bilaspur had been informed about the defect of the notice under Rule 3(3) of Rules 4(2) of Madhya Pradesh Mandal Praja Parishad (Pre separation, Revision & Publication of electoral Rolls and selection of Councillors). [493D] 2:2. The word "may" in Rule 4 has to be interpreted in a broad sense and not in narrow or pedantic sense. It is not the function of the Court to interpret the words used in the statute so as to give them meaning which would have given them a meaning which will have the effect of giving them a retrospective operation. [495G H] 2(a) The word 'may ' has been used in Rule 3 of the Rules to mean "shall" and not merely "may". It is an expression of wide import. It must be interpreted as intended to give it a meaning, which would include all things that are necessary for the proper functioning of the authority. [595G] 2 (b) The Collector has been informed by the petitioners that their names had been included in Annexure P 7 and that they were not aware immediately after the publication of the said notice. It was notified that the nomination could be made on or before November 25. 1978. The notification under Rule 5(1), however, did not specify any time limit for filing the nominations. [504H; 505A] 2.(c) The expression "may", in Rule 5 has to take its colour from the context and purpose of Rule 4 (2). It is a well settled principle that the word 'shall ' must be construed as meaning 'shall'. In the instant case, the Collector had asked for petitioner No. 1 to file his claim for the inclusion in his electoral roll on October 19, 1978 more than two months before the date on which he was informed of it. The petitioners were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored. [506F G] 2)2. In view of the fact that the period of 20 days had been mentioned in the notification issued under rule 4(3), the entire electoral process had became vitiated on the basis of the defective electoral roll '. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High Courts as there was no satisfactory explanation for the delay. [ 505G H; 505B] 2 3.1 In view thereof, the writ petitioner was rightly rejected by the Deputy Collector, Durg and the Collector could not have been allowed to proceed on the footing that the electoral process has become vitiated because of the defects in the notices issued under r. 4(i) of Rule 3 (3). [505C] 3.2 The High court had rightly dismissed the petition as there is no satisfactory evidence for the delayed filing of the petition.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. The balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company were laid before the general body, but the balance sheet did not contain any provision for the closure of the business. The company filed a complaint against the directors for failure to comply with section 220(1) of the . The appellant contended that the provisions of section 220 (2) of 1956 were not applicable to the case and that the company was liable under section 134 of the 1913 Act or section 220 of the Act as the company had failed to call the general meeting. The High Court held that the directors could not rely on their failure to call a general body meeting as a defence to the prosecution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The provisions of sections 132 and 134 of 1956 are not applicable in the present case. Section 132(2) makes it clear that after balance sheet is laid before a general meeting, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted or of complying with the requirements of the Sub section (2). [426 C] (2)(a) The provision under section 220 is mandatory and not directory. It is only in cases where the provisions are not complied with even then the person concerned would be liable for punishment under other provisions of the Indian Penal Code. [427 D E] (b) Section 132 makes it obligatory to send a copy of the balance sheets or profit and Loss account before an annual general meeting is made obligatory. But section 134 lays down that after the balancesheet and profit & loss account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, have been laid before any general body and for not sending a statement of the fact that the balance Sheet was not adopted. [413 D E; 413 A B] (c) The words "in respect of which the balance-sheet is laid" in section 132(1)(3) are clear enough to make him liable under the provisions Of section 134.

The State Government of Hyderabad, by a notification dated January 28, 1950, directed that certain offences or classes of cases should be tried by Special Courts constituted under the Act. The appellant who was one of the accused in the case filed an application before the High Court for a direction to the Special Court to try those offences or class of cases as the case may be. The High Court held that the Special Courts had no jurisdiction to try these offences and directed the Special Judge to frame charges against the appellant under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950. The State Government appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the object of the Act was to provide for speedier trial of certain offences and classes of offences or cases as may be specified in the notification issued under the section. The object of a statute is to show that it is based on a reasonable classification of the persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it is to apply, and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The Act does not provide for the speediers trial but only provides for the procedure to be followed by Special courts. The provisions of section 5 (1) are intended to provide that those cases and offences which in their view require speedian trial must be tried before a special court according to the special procedure provided by it for the purpose of the trial of such offences or offences or both, or class or classes thereof, or classes or of cases or classes as may, in its opinion, require a speediee trial. The provision for the provi sions of the impugned Act is not intended to be an exception to article 14 and must therefore be read as enabling the State Government to direct that those offences and offences should be committed by a Special Court according to such special procedure.

The appellant was a Radiologist in the Medical College of Delhi. He had been working as Radiologist cum Associate Professor of Radiology (ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Maulana Azad Medical College. The appellant was appointed as Radiologists cum Associate Professors of Radiotherapy (exofficio) in the Irwin Hospital which is a teaching hospital attached to the MaHUNG Hospital. He was also promoted as Radiological Surgeon cum Associate professor of Radiologist (exclusively for the purpose of teaching post). In the year 1966, he had been appointed as radiologist cum Assistant Professor of radiotherapy and was confirmed in the post of Radiologists (executive) both under the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules, 1966. The Government of India, Ministry of Health & Family Planning, Department of Health by its letter dated February 23, 1974 informed the Delhi Administration that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the post as Associate Professor in the MahuNG Hospital because he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in Radiotherapist (exoth) in a teaching institution. The respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said order of the Government and contending that the post was not an Associate Professor but a research post and that he had the essential educational qualification and had also the requisite teaching experience while holding the post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent No 1 possessed the qualifications and experience requisite for appointment as Assistant Professors in the M.D.M.S. (extituted) and that the said post was a clinical post while that of Associate Professor and Assistant Professor in a research college. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The post of Associate professor is a clinicalpost though it may be an isolated post but it cannot be equated with a teaching post. [802C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had been substantively appointed to the said posts in the respondent Institute as a Radiologists and was also confirmed in that post. He has been continuously working as such for more than 17 years. The fact that he was not holding a non clinical post in a Teaching hospital like the Irin Hospital is not conclusive of his claim that he possessed the qualification and experience prescribed by the Central Government. [902C D] 1:3. The post is a Clinical post while the appellant has been substantively employed as Associate professor or Associate Professor. The mere designation of the Appellant as an Assistant Professor cum Associate Prof. of Radiological Sciences (ex Assessed) (ex demise) with effect from October 9, 1964 cannot be taken into consideration. [1002C E] 1 4.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of workmen. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 95 per month. In the year 1962, the Company made an application to the Industrial Tribunal for fixation of minimum wage in respect of certain categories of workers. The Tribunal fixed the minimum wage of the workmen at Rs. 90 per month and dearness allowance at Rs., 75 per month for the rest of the employees. The appellant challenged the award on the ground that it was contrary to the principles laid down by this Court in French Motor Car Co. Ltd. vs Its Workmen, ; , that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to fix minimum wage for the workmen. Held: (i) The Tribunal committed an error of law in holding that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs 95 as the average minimum wage prevailing in other industries in the region. [678C] (ii)The Tribunal was right in holding, that the minimum wages were fixed at Rs 95 per day and dearness allowances were ignored. The award was not a rigid one and it was not open to the Tribunal to depart from its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. The question whether the minimum Wages should be fixed at the average level of wages in other comparable industries in that region or not, was not an inflexible one. [688C D] (iii)The award was based on a consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties and it did not require any interference by this court. The tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and there was not and there could possibly not be a claim for higher bonus on the basis of the application of the Full Bench Formula. [698C E] (iv)The principle laid down in French Transport Car Co., Ltd. 's case, is that the formula which is being applied is the simple one of calculating the bonus payable at the rates of three months basic wages and dearness Allowance. The formula is not a static one but is a dynamic one. It is a flexible one. The principle is that it should be applied to all industrial establishments in India irrespective of their respective status or status. [708C F] (v)The question whether there was any justification for departure from the figures of Rs 92 as the minimum pay of the workman was not justified on the principles contained in French Establishments Act, 1947. The fact that the workmen were given a fixed wage at the time of the award shows that they are providing some amenities which are different from those that are being provided by those concerns in the country. [718C G] (vi)The tribunal committed an illegality in holding the minimum rate of wages payable at three months ' basic wages in each case and in no case was the dearness allowance taken into account. The High Court erred in holding otherwise. [72A B] (vii)The fact that there were some clerical staff which did not get any dearness allowance is not conclusive as to whether they are paid minimum wages or not. The only point argued before this Court was that the bonus should be worked out on the basic wage, because it cannot be assumed that their wage is a consolidated wage consisting of the two elements of basic wage and dearness accommodation lumped together. [738C H] (viii)The High Court committed an erroneous error in holding on the evidence that there had been no justification to introduce a new element of payment of bonus to casual and badIi workers at this stage. The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was based upon the evidence which was not challenged before the High Court. [748C C] (ix)The finding of the Tribunal is based on the appreciation of evidence adduced before it and is not perverse.

The assessee, a partnership firm, had entered into contracts with the Government of Bihar for the assessment year 19 19. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee 's income under section 147 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The report submitted by the Income tax officer to the Commissioner was vague and indefinite. It could not be said that he as a result of information in his possession had reasons to believe that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment for that year. [446 B] (ii) The material that he had before him for issuing notice under section 148 is not mentioned in the report. Before issuing a notice under Section 148, the Income Tax Officer must have either reasons to suspect that by reason of omission or failure on the part of these assessee to make a return under section 139 for any assessment year to the income tax Officer or to disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary for his assessment for the accounting year in question. [449 C] (iii) The statement submitted by him under section 151, which is not referred to in the Report, was not produced. It was not a fit case for the issue of a notice unders. 148. [453 D E] (iv) The order sheet recording the reasons of the Incometax Officer as required by section 148(2), was not furnished.

The appellant was a partner in a firm which was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. K.K.S. Piece goods and Yarn Mer chants, Sait Nagjee Purushotham and Co., Bankers, Piece Goods and Yarns, Saits, P Barium Merchants, Paily goods and Karthickam. The firm was dissolved on April 1, 1939 by a decree of the court of the District Judge, Alipore. On March 28, 1939, the appellant filed an application under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1948 49, claiming that there was discontinuance of the business in respect of which he had been assessed as a partner and that the income, profits and gains of the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28. The Income tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the firm was not liable to pay tax under section 26(3) of Act of 1918. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal which held that as a result of the splitting up there was a discontinuance of his original business at the date of partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under section 10(4)(a). On reference, the High Court held that since the firm had been dissolved by a dissolution of the partnership, no tax could be payable by the first mentioned person in respect thereof. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the partners constituting the appellant at the moment of the partition and the subsequent succession to the business were liable to tax as they were not liable under section 23(3); (ii) the partnership was not a dissolved one, and (iii) the firm could not be said to have been assessed to tax in respect o the income profits and losses of the year ending March 28 , 1939. HELD: (i)(a) The partners constituting a firm at the commencement of the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, were liable under the Act of 1922 for the period commencing from April 1 , 1939 and ending on March 28 and the assessment years 1948 49 and 1949 50 would be governed by section 26 of the Act. [107 B] (b) The partnership was dissolved by an agreement between the partners and the firm. It was not necessary that there should be a succession in respect to the income which had paid tax under it for purposes of section 25 (4). [107 C D] (c) The mere fact that he was not taken on in the original business also shows that the original partnership in respect Of which alone the benefit of section 10 (4)(b) can be claimed continued uninterrupted. [108 E F] (d) The firm could have been treated as a dissolved firm only if it had been formed and registered under the Income Tax Act, 1961. The fact that the partners were not taken into account in the previous year also shows the discontinuance of all the businesses.

The appellant, a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener, was the owner of certain properties in his possession. The respondent 's father died in 1947 and his two sons were brought on record as legal representatives. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties by metes and bounds. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the joint property. On appeal, the High Court held that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu coparcenary and that there had been no prior division and that on a true construction of Explanation 1 to section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the interest of a Hindu coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in his property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death. On further consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties, the trial court held that there were six sharers in that property each having one share in it and that, therefore, there was not even a prior partition. The High Court also held that since the appellant 's suit based as it is on the provisions of section 6, was essentially a claim to obtain a share therein immediately before her death, the plaintiff 's share therein will be 1/6th. On an appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: (1) The Explanation 1 which contains the formula for determining the share of the deceased creates a fictional fictional, that the interest in the property that could have been allocated to him when he was entitled thereto, if a family had taken any 1/4th share therein. [724 B] (2) The proviso to section6 resorts to the simple expedient, undoubtedly fictional and is not seriously disputed. It is only in a case where there are six sharer in that land that partition of a coparcenary property can be effected between him and his sons. In such cases, it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain the share which the deceased had in the coparcenary property because after all the plaintiff has a 1/3rd interest in that share. [764 C] (3) The real question for determination is whether there was prior partition or not. If it is the case of the appellant that he was not fully aware of the partition, then he would have got a 1 /4th of the share therein and if he had a 1st share in that partition, he would be entitled to the share so allotted at a notional partition during his life time. [774 C D] (4) The mere fact that the appellant was not aware of any partition effected by him, does not mean that he could have got 1/2th share in a coparcenary. If he had been aware of such a partition, it would be difficult to say that he had no knowledge about the partition. [784 C E] (5) The fact that he has a son is not conclusive proof of his title to the property.

The respondent was appointed as a Clerk in the Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Manager on 1st October, 1956 and was confirmed in that post on 1 st September, 1957. The Corporation issued an order dated 9th December, 1957 appointing him as Assistant Manager with effect from 1st November, 1956, and he was confirmed by the Corporation w.e.f. 1st January, 1960. In the meantime, the Corporation had made a provision for retirement of the respondent on completion of 58 years of age. The respondent challenged the order of his premature retirement before the High Court in a writ petition filed by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employee belonging to Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation was not entitled to continue in service beyond 60 years of the age and that he had been promoted to a class I post or Class III post. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent having the right to continue as Assistant Managers, he could not be reverted to the higher post because he had already completed 58 years; (ii) the Corporation having accepted the offer of appointment made by the respondent and accepted the same, the order terminating his services was illegal and void; and (iii) the High court erred in striking down the regulation 19(2). Dismissing the appeal, this Court. HELD: 1.1 The High Courts erred in holding that a person belonging to class I or class II appointed on or before 1st August, 1956 shall retire on completion Of 58 years ' of age if he has attained the age of 60 years and the appointing authority may extend his service for one year at a time upto 60 years. [319C] 1.2 The High court was wrong in striking out regulation 19. [421D] 1:3. The question whether the age should be raised to 60 years or not is a matter of policy. It is well settled that the power of the Government to extend at any time beyond 58 years is an administrative power and cannot be exercised arbitrarily, arbitrarily or capriciously. [427E] 1(a) The High courts erred in taking into consideration the fact that the respondent had the right of being appointed as Assistant managers on or prior to 1st April, 1956 but only referred to the employees and agents of the State Government who were employed after 1 st October, 1957 and who were appointed subsequent to 1 st August, 1957 by the corporation in respect of whom the Corporation has fixed the age. [521G] (b) The respondent was not a permanent employee of Class I nor was he appointed on 1St September,1956. He had been appointed prior to that date only after 1St October,1957. Therefore, he cannot be said to have continued in service till 60 years as a class III employee by virtue of the settlement and the amendment made in the year 1965. [506G] 2(a). The HighCourt erred in quashing the regulation on the ground that it was not in terms applicable to the respondent. [504H; 506A B] (c) The Corporation had no right to terminate the services of its employees after 1.9.1956 and therefore, the impugned order terminating the services was bad. [ 506B C] (d) The order of termination is illegal and invalid because it has been passed without giving any opportunity to the employee to show cause against the proposed action.

The appellants, who were the Judges of the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order dated December 20, 1975 passed by the Full Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The High Court held that the letter was not an offence under section 3(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and that it did not amount to contempt of court. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Courts have no power to interfere with the matters in question except by way of a writ of certiorari or other appropriate writ. [243E] (ii) The letter dated December 19, 1975 was addressed by the deponent to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned for any reason contempt of Court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. [244E] The High court did not mention which particular portion of the letter constituted contempt of the court. It was no part of the duty of a Judge or Judge to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [245F] (iii) The Full Bench fell into error in accepting the apology without finding that the appellants committed any contempt. [246E] In view of the fact that the High Courts proceeded on the basis that the allegations in the letter were unchallenged, it was not part of its duty to go personally and address the meeting on the political matters. [247A B] (iv) The contempt proceedings are dropped.

The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 under the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore not valid. Held, that the provisions of section 6(4) of Act XXXV of 1947 were ultra vires the powers conferred by article 14 and were void as being violative of articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. The impugned Act did not contravene article 14 Of the Constitution because it violated articles 14 or 19 of its Constitution. The Act was a piece of discriminatory legislation which infringed articles 14, 19 and 31 of the Consti tution. The provisions of the impugned Act were in substance one for the purpose of enabling the person whose case or points in whose case he is or are being investigated to rebut any evidence brought on record against him, he shall, on application made in this behalf and on payment of such fees as may be prescribed by rules, be furnished with certified copies of documents, statements, papers and materials brought on the record by the Commission. The procedure prescribed by the impugned section was a good substitute for that prescribed by article 20(3) of our Constitution. It was not open to the petitioner to contend that the impugned sections were violative of article 14 or were void because they contravened articles 14 Of Constitution. Held further, that in view of article 19(1)(f) of its constitution it is not necessary to consider whether section 6 (4) is ultra vires and invalid. The validity of sub section (4), which was enacted by the Legislature under the provisions contained in article 20 (3) was not challenged on any ground. It could not be said that the Act was void because it contravened articles 19(2) and 31 Of the constitution, as it did not comply with the provisions made in the impugned Acts. The question whether sub section(4), of section 3, which was introduced by the Amending Act, was ultra vires, was one of construction of article 20 of theConstitution and was not a matter for consideration before this Court.

The appellant, a company incorporated in India, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling products. The respondent, a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops & Establishments Act, 1954, was a " commercial establishment". The respondent was a 'Commercial Establishment ' within the definition of Section 2(9) of that Act. The appellant, who was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, was formed and registered as a "Commercial Establishment" in the State of Delhi. The Company was incorporated on April 1, 1957, by virtue of an agreement dated May 5, 1958 entered into between the respondent and its employees. The company was to be governed by the provisions of the Act. Under section 2 (9) the appellant was to carry on business in any place within the jurisdiction of the Company. Section 2 (5) provided that "commercial establishments" shall mean all such establishments as are specified in the Schedule. The respondents were not members of the appellant 's association, but were members of a "industrial establishment". In the year 1958, the respondent was appointed as an Assistant Manager of the company. On June 30, 1959, the appellant filed a complaint against the respondent alleging that it had been carrying on business of selling or disposing of goods in Delhi for a consideration which was not paid by him and that the respondent had no right to sell or dispose of the undertaking of the respondent. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the activity of the Federation was in the nature of a trade, business or profession within the ambit of section2(5). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the activities of the respondents were in the character of trade and business and therefore they were not liable to be prosecuted under section 2 of the . Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The activity of a registered society is a commercial establishment within the purview of section.2(9). [352B] (a) The definition of "commercial Establishment" indicates that the expression "commercial purpose" means any purpose or profession which is carried on in a premises for profit. It does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Federal Court inR. K . Of course that profit was plou ghed back to the purpose of the Association as set out in its Memorandum of Association. [352C D] (b) The word "commercial" has been defined in section 2,(5), in the context of which it is used in the Act and is not distributed among its members. It would bear repetition. the Federation further publishes a periodicals bulletins and issues a to member Free of this court in R, K.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his successors. The income from the property was assessed to agricultural income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income. The Income tax Officer held that it had been a regular business of the Government to provide for the payment of the allowance in respect of the land revenue collection after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the allowance was a permanent one and didnot fall within section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Tribunal held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting cost of Tahsil office. The High Court on reference answered the question in the negative. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The source of the income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of that Act. [710 B] (2) The income of a fractional share of the net income of an assessee is altered when a part of the gross revenue collections is appropriated by him as his remuneration, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the total income. [700 C D] (3) In the instant case, the source of income was clearly the agreement arrived at between the parties. The source and character of the expenditure are, therefore, altered when the income cannot be held to be derived from land within the meaning of section 4 (3)(vii). [711 G H] (4) The High Courts have taken a contrary view in the case of Commissioner of Income tax vs Shah Jiwaji Rao & Co. , and Commissioner of Incometax vs Shahji Khimji, ; , followed.

The petitioners in Civ il Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade II in the various ordnance factories between 1962 to 1966 a nd they had filed writ petitions before this Court challenging their promotion as Chargeman II on completion of two years ' service as Supervisor 'A ' by its order dated 28th December, 1965 and the judgment dated 4th April, 1983. The petitioners contended that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated th at appointments by promotion were to be made on the basis of selection list prepared in the manner provided therei n, there was no scope for automatic promotion merely because the petitioners had been promoted as Chargemen II on expiry of 2 years of continuous service on the ground of their length of service and his promotion thereafter could not be effected only in accordance with the normal Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the respondents were not entitled to have beco rded the chargeman II for promotion merely on completion o f two years of service on their basis of the circular dated 6th November, 1962 and had provided that in future promotions of all such individuals will be effected in accordance wit h the normal rules and not merely on the completion of 2 yea rs satisfactory continuous service. The State appealed to this Court by special leave against the judgment of the High Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have been given the same relief which was granted to the petitioners in the writ petition before the Madhya Pradesh High Court and nearly 2 years ev en after the decision dated 2nd February, 1981 in Civil Appeal No 441 of1981 in CIV il appeal No. 442 of 1981. [106C] 1.2 The HighCourt held that the State Government had not been given a back date promotion to the post of Chargeman I synchronising with the dates of completion of their 2 years ' servi ce as Supervisor "A" by its earlier order dated 6 th November, 1965. The Court further held that it was not open to the respondents to have been granted the same benefit which was extended to the petitioner in Civil appeal No 441/81 and the petitioners of Civi lation were also entitled to be treated as Charge man II by the time their cases could be considered for promo tion. [107D E] 1:3. The Madhya Pradesh Hi gh Court held that since the judgment in Civil Appeals No. 440 of 1981 was not fully complied with, the respondents in Civil appeals No 441 and 442 of 1982 were entitled to the same benefits which were granted to them in Civil 2nd Appeal No 442 of1981.

The appellants, a private operator, were operating tourist vehicles in the State of Karnataka. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court held that the permits granted to the appellants were valid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of some of the private operators that the State Transport Undertaking would have preference over those who had applied for the permit from the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, and that the appellants should be given preference over others. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that of the State Road Transport Appellate tribunal was correct. [1015C] 2.1 In the instant case, the State Government had not considered the merits of the claims of the Karnataka State Road transport Corporation and the private operator who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to section 63(7) of the Act. [1005D] 2:2 The High Courts have failed to consider the merits and the permits of the appellants which were granted by the State transport Undertaking for operating in any inter state route without detriment to its responsibility for providing efficient and adequate road transport services in any notified area or notified route. [102E F] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. 2.3 The High court was right that the decision taken by the High Courts and the State Governments was correct and that it had not been challenged before this Court. [103F] Sher singh 's Case, referred to above, distinguished. 1.2 In the present case, there is no dispute that the private parties were operating in the inter state routes without any right of renewal or any other statutory right. The permits granted by them were valid and they could not be said to have been obtained by them for their own use. [104F] 2(a) The High courts had failed to appreciate the merits in the claims made by the Karnataka Road Transport Corporation and private operators who did neither get a Certificate of approval nor approval from Central Government, because of rule of priority under section 63 (7). [103G H] Sher SINGH vs Union Of India, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R.

The respondent was a dealer in goods. He purchased the business of selling them at Madras and sold it to the appellant. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on the turnover of the appellant for the years 1957 58, 1958 59 and 1959 60. The appellant challenged the levy by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that Rule 21 A was intra vires of the power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that Rule 22A was ultra vires of article 14 of the constitution as it was intra legislative in character and not before. HELD: The High court was right in holding that Rule 23 A is ultra vires the rule making power of State Government. [664 D] (i) The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power to recover tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 20A is beyond the rulemaking power of a State Government either under section 9 or section 10 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. [666 G] (ii) The words 'assessment to be made ' in section 9(2)(a) do not include any power of recovery of tax assessed on the property of the person liable to pay the tax under the Act.[664 D E] (iii) Rule 21A is ultra legislative and cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other similarly situated.

The appellant was a public servant. He was dismissed from service on February 2, 1955. The respondent filed an application under section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 for a declaration that he continued to be in Government service till the date of his suit only and there will be a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not entitled to any salary for the period of suspension. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against the plaintiff. [922 B] (2) The State of Bombay admitted that the plaintiff was not supplied with a copy and had not been prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of his report. The State 's failure to supply the copy did not affect the validity of the suit. [990 C D] (3) The judgment of the High Court is set aside and the decree passed by the trial court decreeing the suit is restored. [992 B] The State Government was entitled to recover arrears of salary from the appellant on the ground that he had not asked for copy of a report of enquiry held by the Enquiry Officer. [963 C] (4) The finding of the trial Court that there was breach of Article 311(1) of Constitution is correct and must be set aside.

The plaintiffs and the defendant were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama. The plaintiffs claimed that they had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side of the colliery, that the defendants had encroached on the land in dispute and removed coal from the encroached portion of the coal mine. The trial court held that the defendant had encroached over the coal of the plaintiff 's lease, but the High Court accepted the finding of the Subordinate Judge that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that they were aware of the removal of coal by the defendants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts erred in holding that the burden of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on them and that they would be entitled to the reliefs prayed for. Held, that under the Indian Mines Act and the Rules framed thereunder the plaintiffs were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the defendant 's working and, therefore, the coal that was left in the encroached area was not by any means accessible to the plaintiffs and being thus wholly unworkable is entirely lost to them for ever. The High Court was right in holding on the assumption that the initial burden of proving knowledge on a party to the encroachment only within three years of the suit was on the appellant, but it had failed in its duty to prove the fact that they came to know of the damage only within 3 years of their possession of the converted property and that is all. The appellant had not denied the fact and stated that the respondents were aware and had been aware of this encroachment only in the year 1941 which was within three yeans from 1932.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was charged with misconduct under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders and was dismissed from service. The respondent challenged the dismissal order in a writ petition before the High Court which was allowed.
