In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the termination of service because the employer wanted to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r 18(b) of Standing Orders. HELD : (i) The appellant could not be said to have acted under r, 18(1) in as much as that rule was used to get rid of an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct, notice for which had been given to the employee and for which a departmental inquiry was intended to be held. [14 E] (ii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the exercise of power under r 17(a), of the standing orders was colourable exercise of the power conferred on the appellant and therefore its action could not have been upheld as a bona fide exercise of it. [15 G H] (iii) The employer could defend the action under r 19(a). But in a case where the employer desired to take action for misconduct actually charged might be done away with, the employer could not question the causes that led to the termination. [16 E F] (iv) The tribunal was right when it held that the action taken under the Standing orders was bona fide and was not colourable exercise or victimisation. [17 G H; 18 A B] (v) The question whether the action of the employer was bona fides or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice is a mixed question of fact and law. It is well settled that in an industrial dispute relating to termination of employment of an employees, the appropriate Government has to decide whether there was in fact misconduct or not. [18 G H, 18 A] (vi) The word 'employee ' in r. 19(1)(a) means a person who is employed for wages and includes a person employed on any day of the month during which he is employed. In the present case, the tribunal held that there was no misconduct or victimisation as the employer had not taken action under the standing Orders.

The respondent, a tenant of the appellant 's premises, filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that it was entitled to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit and directed the appellant to pay Rs. 1,000/ as costs. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the question whether the agreement dated December 1, 1960 created a lease or not was a lease and that the consent decree operated as res judicata. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the agreement between the parties was barred by the principle of res judicata under section 92 of the Evidence Act, because the question was already concluded by the consent decrees in suit No. 149 of 1960 and that in view of the consent Decree in suit no question of resjudicata could be raised. HELD: (i) The High Court has recorded a finding that the agreement of November 27, 1954 created a tenancy. [446 B] (ii) The question whether a contract is a lease was not a matter to be decided by the Court and on which the opinion of witnesses was irrelevant. It was not open to the Court to express any opinion about the rights and contentions of the parties with reference to the agreement. [427 C D] (iii) The consent decree in suit Nos. 149 and 149 of 1961 had not decided that the contract between the appellant and respondent No. 1 was a tenancy or other character had to be determined at the trial and the previous judgment being a judgment by consent, it could not operate as resjudicata. [545 C] (iv) The agreement dated November 27. 1954 created an agreement of lease and therefore the consent order in suit was set aside. [ 428 D E] (v) The Court proceeded to observe that the parties had been given full opportunity to lead evidence and put questions to them before the Court. It is not open for the Court, on principle, to express its opinion about rights and claims of the party with reference thereto. But it was not decided in Major section Khanna 's case(1) that every order of the Court in the course of a suit amounts to a lease. [ 429 C D]. (vi) The decision of the High court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed on 1st June, 1983. He was declared unfit by a Medical Board and was re quired to be reinstated in service with effect from 30th August, 1985. The petitioner filed a Writ Petition before the High Court challenging the order of termination of his services. The High Court held that the termination order could not be sustained and the Writ Petition was liable to be dismissed. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that he was entitled to be paid salary upto the period he was allowed to remain in service. Dismissing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The respondent had not urged before the Court that the order dated 24.3.1988 entitled him to be reinstatement in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th of August,1985 or not. If the respondent was really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24th March 1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that he did not do so. [243C D] 2. The order of appointment issued in his case was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30th Aug., 1985 were liable to been ignored and that the petitioner should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to remain In service. [244E F] 3. The Court had, therefore, to consider whether the respondent is entitled to continue in service beyond 30. August, 1986 unless there was a further extension. If it was really challenged by the respondent he proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be re quire in service even though there was no order of extension of service. If he did so, he should not have been reinstated in his service till 30.8.1985 when the order was passed. [245E F; 246A] 4. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respondent be treated to be a person regular in Government Service entitled to retain till he completed the age of 58 years. His only case was that the interim order conferred on him a right to continue as in service upto 30th September, 1985 when the orders of termination were liable for cancellation or re quires. He should have been treated as an employee regularly appointed and no observations in this regard were made by the Court. [246B C] 5. The writ petition was not maintainable because it did not raise any question of law nor was it right in making an order on review on 26.7.1988 relying upon the interim orders dated 10.7,1986 which in the circumstances could not have the effect of controlling the jurisdiction of the High Courts to dispose of the Writ Petitions on merits as it did on 24. 3.1988.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of life imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove the motive of the crime beyond reasonable doubt and that the discrepancies in the evidence were of a minor character. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The discrepancies on the basis of which the Trial Court rejected the evidence of P.W. 1 to 3 and the evidence Of the defence and when two views were possible, the benefit of doubt should be given to the accused. [367E] 2.1 The High Courts have not been justified in rejecting the evidence on the ground that the discrepancy was caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [368E] 3.2 The discrepancies in evidence are of a major character and they have been so strong against a man as to leave only a remote possibility in his favour which can be dismissed with the sentence of course it is possible but not in the least probable. [369F] 3(a) There is no reason why an injury of the nature received by the deceased could have been caused in any manner in the way suggested by him. The injury must have was caused at the time suggested by P. W. 1. [370G] (b) The discrepancies are of minor character and that they have not occurred in a minor nature. It has to be remembered that the injuries on the person of the accused could have taken place at 10 p.m. when the victim was lying down on her left side. There is nothing short of that will suffice.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as an Additional District Judge in January, 1973. He was removed from his office by an order dated May 27, 1974. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that the appellant had not been given any opportunity to defend himself and that he had not availed of the opportunity afforded to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts were not competent to issue a writ of certiorari under article 227 of the constitution, because the High court could not have issued a writ in respect of an order passed by the Chief Justice of India under Article 124(4) of the Consti tution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power to punish a subordinate Judge is not necessarily conferred on him by the Constitution and it is for this reason that such constitutional functionaries do not fall within the purview of the Act. [216C] 2.1 The High Courts are not competent under article 136 read with Article 226 of Constitution to issue any writ of mandamus or other appropriate writ, calling for the records relating to the proceedings before them and to quash the order passed in the present case. [217D] 2(a) The power conferred on the Supreme court by section 6(1)(c) is not confined to a Judge who has been removed from office by the President under article 124(5). It is for that authority to decide whether or not the person removed from the office of Chief Justice should be removed from such office by any other authority. [218F] 2 (b) The word "office" in section 6 (1)(d) has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of the competent authority under Section 6(2) of Act. It is not necessary that the authority concerned should have any power of superintendence even over the High courts Judges but it must be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. [212F] 3(a). The word 'office ' in section 2(b) has been used in wide sense, but it has not been defined in the Act or in any other enactment. It has been held by this Court that the expression "office of Chief justice" in clause (e) of sub section (1) of Section 6 is not restricted to a person who holds such office. [213F] In the instant case, the word 'officer ' has been defined under section 2 (c) as the only punishment; and a special law enacted by Parliament under Article 13 read with article 124 of theConstitution for removal of a Judge. The word `office ' has to have its meaning in clause(e) thereof. [214H] 3.1 In the present cases, the HighCourt was not competent either to appoint or to remove a person from office as Chief Justice or of the High Commission under Article 217(4). [214A B] 3 (b). The expression 'office of chief justice ' in clause 2(c) has not to be read in any manner whatsoever. It cannot be said that the word `officer ' is used in the sense of a person holding such office, but the word "officer" has been given a restricted meaning which will place the onus on the prosecuting agency to prove that he was holding such an office. The expression `office of a Chief Justice ' in Clause 2(d) of Article 124 means only his removal from office in the manner provided in clause 3(b).

The appellant was a Sunri by caste. He belonged to a smaller caste group of Sunri caste which had nothing to do with Sunri. The respondent 's case was that the appellant belonged to an independent caste and not a member of any Scheduled Caste. The Tribunal held that the respondent belonged to the "Scheduled Castes" and not to "other Backward Classes". On appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was right in holding that the Respondent had established that the Appellant belonged to 'the smaller caste groups within the Sunri ' group and did not belong to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. [389C] (2) The appellant was not a person belonging to the Schedule Caste specified under item 40 of the Schedule. The appellant could not be said to have been a member or a member thereof. [390E F] (3) The respondent had not established that he belonged to any other caste which was clearly independent of the Suniti caste group. [391F G] (4) The finding of the Tribunal that the 'appellant belonged to "Scheduled Caste" is correct and it was open to the respondent to show that the said appellant belonged in the larger caste group within the fold of Sunari caste. [392H; 392A] (5) The High Court was right, on a proper construction of item 40, that it indicated men of theSunri caste but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste Group of Sahas.

The appellant was a tenant of the premises in dispute. The rent was Rs. 1,000 and the rent was paid to the complainant. The appellant asked for a sum of Rs. 29,500 as compensation for the loss suffered by him on account of the failure of the complainant to pay the amount. The complainant refused to accept the said sum. Thereupon the appellant filed a complaint against the respondent under section 19(2) of the , and the Magistrate took cognizance of the offence. The High Court held that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition of the relin quishment by a tenant, of his tenancy and that the appellant was not entitled to claim compensation for loss suffered in respect of the said amount. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the word "relinquish" used in section 18(1) of Act is wide enough to include within its ambit any person who has committed default in payment of rent or damages for use and occupation of the property. The word "related person" is not defined in the Transfer of Property Act. It is a well settled rule that when an agreement is made by one party to another, it is not necessary that the parties must be related to each other. In the present case there was no such intention on the part of the appellant to the transfer of the flat and the possession was delivered to him. The mere fact that the respondent had agreed to pay Rs. 30,000 as compensation did not make any difference in the position. The agreement was not a term of art and was used in the section not in any strict technical sense but in its comprehensive meaning as giving up of possession of the land.

The appellant, a contractor in the State of Maharashtra, was engaged as a contractor for the construction of a building. The work of the contractor was to be done by the contractor himself and his employees were to be paid wages at the rates prescribed by the Government from time to time. The contractor was also paid Rs. 100/ per month as compensation for the loss suffered by him in the execution of the works contract. The appellant, who was a contractor with the respondent company, was charged with the work of construction of the building and the contractor had been paid a sum of Rs. 150/ . The respondent company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the award on the ground that it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contract was fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (1) that the existing wage scales were fair and adequate; (2) that there was no justification for the increase in the basic pay of individual workman; (3) that it could not be said that the respondent had been discriminated against in respect of the workmen who were paid higher wages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of the Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the award of all the employees in the category of Draftsmen and Rs. 200/ is confirmed. [306D] 2.1 The basic pay was fixed at Rs.150/ per day. It was not a case of any increase in wages or additional financial liability. The increase was made on account of the rise in the cost of construction work. The Tribunal was wrong in making the award dated December 20, 1978. [307E] 2(a) The Tribunal had no power to make an award on a particular date and it could only modify the basic wage of individual workmen by increasing the minimum wages payable to each workman. It could not have made any reference to the Tribunal for fixing the wage structure. [308F] 3.2 In the instant case, the Tribunal was conscious that the increase of Rs 150/ in the scale of Draughtsmen and the Rs.100/ in other categories would be fair and proper. The financial capacity as the Tribunal observed was found to be very much more than the increased wage of each workman who belonged to the Union staff.

The appellant was a contractor. He paid wages to the respondents as per the award of the Industrial Tribunal. The respondents contended before the High Court that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant not to pay the wages. The High Court held that section 2(vi) includes wages prescribed by the Industrial Disputes Act and so it had rejected the appellants contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section 15 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The provisions of the , are applicable to industrial adjudication in terms of section 2 (vi). [447 D] (ii) The words "as the case may be" occurring in section 2 of the . are wide enough to include wages prescribed under the Industrial Tribunals Act. The words 'as the circumstances of the case ' in section 3(vi), refer to the circumstances in which the award or settlement is made and not to those cases where the terms of the contract of employment have been violated. [448 D] In the instant case, the respondents contended that the application made by the respondents was incompetent under s 15 of Act. They were therefore entitled to the benefit of section 15. [427 G H] (iii) The question whether the wages prescribed in an award are "as" defined by section 2, is not well founded. It is now well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms thereof, a contract between the parties, though express or implied, is one of them. [545 B] (iv) The terms prescribed by an award cannot be treated as wages under section 2. In fact, it is not so in the present case. It was not shown to the satisfaction of the Tribunal that they constitute part of the terms and conditions of employment either express or implicit.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the trial Magistrate. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the accused had committed an offence either under section 465 or section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution which resulted in conviction of the accused was initiated without any sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and if sanction under that section is necessary, as contended for by him, the question whether sanction under s. 197(I) of Cr. P.C. is necessary when the act complained of attached to the official character of the person doing it, those which had held that it was necessary in all cases in which the official integrity of the public servant gave him an opportunity for the commission of the crime, and those who had held the office of a public servant must be deemed to have been guilty of such offence; (2) the sanction under sub section (1), of section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was necessary when it was sought to be prosecuted without any previous sanction under the section. HELD : (i) The prosecution which has resulted in the conviction of appellant was initiated by the Public Work Department without any authority under section 196(1). [1306 D] (ii) The sanction under Section 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure is not necessary if it is necessary for the prosecution to prove its case. It is only when the offence complained of is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have existed on the merits and could not arise at the stage of the grant of sanction which mu t precede the institution of the prosecution. [1307 D] The question whether the act of criminal misappropriation or forgery has been brought home to the appellant or not is a matter relevant at the point of sanction. [1408 E F] (iii) The mere fact that the offence was directly concerned in his official duty so that if questioned it could not be said to have taken place on account of any previous act, the acts with which the appellant is charged would fall within the scope of his duties and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. [1509 E F; 1510 A] (iv) The fact that a public officer who has been prosecuted under s 409 of Indian Penal code is not required to obtain sanction for prosecution under section 198(1), Cr.P.C., does not mean that he can be said, when charged with it, to have committed an act which is directly connected with his office and so on. [1609 E] (v) The absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecutions.

The appellant was a resident of Travancore State in the year 1949. He filed returns for the assessment years 1949 50 and 1950 51 showing his income as business losses during the previous year. The Income tax Officer, on an application under section 4(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, assessed the appellant to income tax on the profits and gains of the two years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile State of Travancore were not taxable as income under section 3 or the provisions of section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (1) the first proviso to section 24(1)(Per Bose, J.) did not apply to the case because the words " business in British India" in section 24 were used only to indicate that where the loss sustained is a loss of profits and gain which would but for the loss have accrued or arose within British India, the loss could be deducted from profits made in British Indian State. (2) The mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be set off against profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India and the Indian States, did not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits or gains arising within British Indian territory only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1941, and not under section 24 (1)(per Bose J.) (3) The words "business in BritishIndia" in the proviso to sub section (1), did not support the construction.

The appellant company was incorporated in Calcutta. The Company had its registered office at Calcutta and its branches offices were situated at Calcutta. In the year 1958, the Company made an agreement with its employees for retirement of their employees at 60 years subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. The company however did not agree to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at 60. In September 1959, an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age for the workmen of the respondent was extended to 58 years subject only to the employees passing a Medical examination on coming to know that there was no medical examination. The appellant company also made an application for fixing the age at 60 in the year 1959. The Tribunal held that the age was fixed at 60 and not at 55. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had failed to notice that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement age at 58 years. [427 G] (ii) The award of the Tribunal is set aside and the matter remitted back to it for fresh consideration. [447 B C] (iii) The Industrial Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the appellant was entitled to fix his age at 55 or at 58. [545 D] (iv) The finding of the tribunal that in all the awards in recent times in Bombay, there were no uniform practice of fixing the retirement at 62 years is erroneous and cannot be sustained. [ 428 E F] (v) The appellant 's claim for fixing age of retirement at 55 was under negotiation. There is nothing to show that the industry cum region basis had been fixed for fixing retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60, and the Tribunal has failed to see any recent trend in this regard. [ 429 D E] (vi) The awards and agreements on the question of age of superannuation are wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal had done was that there were a consistent trend in the Bombay region to fix retirement age for clerical and inferior staff at 61.

The first respondent, a company incorporated in the United Kingdom, was appointed as the managing director of the appellant company. The first respondent was appointed by the Board of Directors of the company as its managing director. The second respondent was also appointed as an managing director and the third respondent was nominated as the Managing Director. The appellant filed a petition under section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956 for the appointment of a new managing director in place of the first respondent. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the first Respondent had no authority to appoint the second respondent as its Managing Director and that the second Respondent was not competent to appoint him as the Director. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the Company was being conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members or any other persons or persons or otherwise for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose; and (2) that the Board had no power to appoint its Managing director as its Director. HELD : (i) The first Respondent was appointed the managing Director of the Appellant company as his managing director on February 6, 1964. The appointment of the second appellant as the Chairman of the Board was administrative in character and could not be questioned by him under section 235(1). [323 B] (ii) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative that it can delegate its function under section 236 to the Board but it has no power of delegation. It may be mentioned that in paragraph 16 of the affidavit the Chairman also stated: "With reference to paragraph 21 of the petition, I have already stated that there was sufficient material before the Board on which it could and did form the opinion that there are circumstances suggesting any of these things and not whether they establish any of those things.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The High Court confirmed their conviction but acquitted them of the charge under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 1,000/ . On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption that they were dacoits could not be drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, according to which dacoity was committed at the time of dacoity was found in their houses. HELD : (i) The presumption under section 114 of the has been drawn and in the present case it is not necessary to state specifically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is, too large, the presumption would be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case. [723 D E] (ii) The fact that the appellants were found in possession of stolen property at the relevant time of the dacoity was a piece of evidence which connects them further with the crime. It is difficult to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen Property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [700 D E; 700 A] (iii) The time gap between the time when the discovery was made and the actual place of occurrence is a small one which connectes him further with crime.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ' within Rule 2(x)(2) of the , filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to include in the list of substances included in the Rules as "Poisons" and to declare that the substance as poison was an absolute one. The petitioners contended that since the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory appli cation as it is left to each State Government for determining what substance they would include as poison, and that the impugned notification dated April 1, 1919 was not in accordance with law. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners were manufacturers 'thine arsenic, the expanded its provisions and enabled the State Govern ment to declare any substance as an poison for the purpose of the Act by a notification under the Act or the rules made thereunder. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the enactment is to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. It does not require that the same substance should be declared as poison for purposes of the Central Act. [222C] 2.1 The expression "poison" in Rule 2 (x)(ii) of Rules, 1926 is used in a sense of wide import. The word "po ison" has been defined in the General Clauses Act, 1897 to mean any substance specified as a poison in a rule or noti fication issued under the . [222G] 2(i) The expression 'poisin ' means any substance which the Government consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulat ed in the interest of health and safety of the society. It is not necessary that the said substance should he declared as an insecticide for the purposes of section 2(xi). [222H; 223A] 2.(ii) The word 'poise ' has been used in the context of Rule 2. The expression includes any substance mentioned as a pesticide in a Rule or notifica tion issued under it. [223B] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioners are manufacturers of "thiner" within Rule 1(x) and there is nothing to show that they were not declared as insecticides for the entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance ance as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that area and the need to regu late the possession of the poison for sale and the sale of the specified poison. [224D] 3(i)(ii). The notification, and its applications to any areas would depend upon the necessity for declaring the substance a poison on a particular facts. [225E F] 3.(iii) The notification is not in consonance with the provisions of the . The notification does not contain any provision which makes it obligatory for the State to regulate its possession under section 2 (xi). The petitioners are not entitled to the benefit of the notification because they are manufacturers 'donation ' within r. 2(xii)(2). [225G] 3 (iv) The Notification and its Application to any other area would be governed by the provisions contained in Rule 1 of the Rules.

The assessee firm was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1954 54. The Income tax Officer, on a reference made under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, assessed the amount of Rs. 2,68,385/ as irrecoverable debt due from the Bombay firm. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal held that the debt of Rs 2, 68,385 was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that there were three important circumstances which appear from the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Income tax officer from which it may be inferred that the advances made by the appellants to the Bombay Firm were not in respect of loans in the ordinary course of the business of their firm. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that the debts of Rs, 2,69,385 were not one arising in the case of a loan advanced in the normal course of its business of a assessee. [12 E] (ii) The expression "accommodation" is used in section 10(2)(xi) and it includes a debt which is capable of being created by means of a contract or arrangement, but does not include a debt representing loss sustained in the other business. [13 F G] (iii) The word "accommodity" has been defined in section 2(11) to mean any thing which is not capable of creating a debt and includes a charge on property. It means a debt as defined in the Act, whether it be an actionable claim or not. [14 A B] (iv) The words "accharged" are used in the context of the definition of "accuminous debt". The word 'accommodated ' is used to mean a debt or doubtful debt which has been created by a contract with the object of creating such debt. It does not mean a loan or an actionable claims. [15 C] (v) The term "acccotic" in section 3(2) of Act, 1962, means a loan and a debt includes a liability to pay interest on it. The word is used for the purpose of defining the expression 'accommodation '. It is not defined in any statute. It has been used in a sense of the term as meaning a thing which may be regarded as a thing capable of producing a thing or a thing.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the said lands in terms of section 36 of the Land Acquisition Act. The High Court granted stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the lands in question. In these petitions under Article 136 of the Constitution, the petitioners contended that as the awards were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the Act, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [565E] 2. The question whether the awards are made within one year from September 20, 1984 or not is a matter to be decided by the High Court and if it is found that they are not relevant for deciding the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. [567F G] 3. The object of Section 11 A is to provide for the award of compensation in respect thereof. It is well settled in law that the relief under Article 226 of the constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with clean hands. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [568F G; 567A] 4. The writ petitions are accordingly dismissed. There will be no order as to costs of these petitions.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the Bank on January 1, 1959. He was drawing basic pay at Rs. 12 per month and his basic pay was fixed at Rs.. 901/ per month. The appellant was paid dearness allowance at the rate of Rs. 10 per month for the period from January 1 to March 31, 1962. On April 1, 1963 the appellant made an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, claiming that he should be given increments in the scale provided by the Sastry award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal on May 2, 1964. The respondent contended that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the said award and that the workmen were entitled to increments under sub cl. (b) of cl. 10 of the Sastry Award. The Industrial Tribunal held that the workman was entitled only to the benefits of increment in the scales provided by cl. 5(d) of the Desai award and directed payment of Rs.. 1,000/ per year as dearness allowance. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The appellant 's basic pay as on January 31, 1959 was Rs. 901 // per annum and he was entitled for increments under section 32A of that Act. The Tribunal had rightly held that he was not entitled to any benefit under the award. (ii) The workmen were not entitled for increment in scale provided they were drawing basic salary at a particular stage in the time scale of the scales of pay as modified from that stage onwards. (iii) The Tribunal was right in holding that the respondent was entitled, on the basis of the award, to increments in scale prescribed by cl.(a). (iv) The award was not liable to be set aside on the ground that it had been passed without giving any opportunity to the workmen to show cause why they should not be paid. (v) The Award was not a speaking one and could not be challenged as being violative of section 33(A)(b) because the award was made in 1962 and the award had been made in 1963.

The land of the extent of four acres was carved out and given to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of five Star Hotel. The Government of West Bengal appeared to have been on the search for two suitable plots of land which could be offered, one to the I.T.D.C., and the other to the Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. The land was allotted to the T.D., C.B.C. and the Taj group of Hotels. The appellant 's application for allotment of a larger plot of land was rejected by the Government on the ground that it had no nexus with the object of the Zoo. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the decision to lease the Begumbari land to the G.T.,D.B.,C.B.; and the Indian Railways should point out that the Zoom Group of hotels in Calcutta had been formed for the purpose of providing a Five Star Hotel, and that the land allotted to it was not used for the main purpose of the zoo for the development of a Five star hotel. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of thezoo when they decided to grant four acres of Begumbar land which was not use for the principal purpose of Zoo for construction of a five Star hotel. [261C] 1.2 The fact that the GT., D.B,C.L. and other hotels had been on lease hold basis, would not make any difference to the question whether the construction was in the eating, the land being allotted to them for the hotel. The fact of the fact that they were leased out to the Government of Bengal did not justify an inference that the construction had been made in the appellant ' s premises. [262D] 1:3. The principle of price in the open market would be wholly inept, because in view of the State Policy, there would be no question of any resin being sold in the public interest. [263F G] 1 4.1 In a case like this where the State is allo cating resources such as water, power raw materials etc. for the purposes of encouraging setting up industries within the State, we do not think that the State was bound to advertise and tell the people that it wants a particular industry to be set up within the state and invite those interested to come up with pro posal. On a consideration of all the facts and circumstances of the case, the Government would have to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price, subject, of course, to any other relevant overriding considerations of public weal or interest. But in a case where the Government is all o cating materials such as Water, power input material etc. which may have to be taken into account by the State in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the Court would have jurisdiction to decide whether the action of the Government was reasonable and in public interest and not public interest [263G H; 264A] 1 5.1 ought to point out whether this is one of the exceptional cases where the state has made available to this court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of the state government land to respondent No. The matter was taken in appeal. "The Division Bench held that the decisions taken were neither unreasonable nor arbitrary and that taking away of four acre of land from the Zoor was not detrimental to public interest". [264C D] 1 6.2 In view of State Policy the Court should have decided whether the actions of the government are reasonable and, in public interests.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in gold and silver. The Income Tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58 on the ground that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.1,50,000 on 1.1.1957. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs.67560/12/ was rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Tribunal also held that there was no completed gift of the value of Rs, 50,000 to his son. In reference under section 27(1) of the Act, the High Court held that it was not open to the Tribunal 's right to hold that the amount of Rs 1,50.,000 was rightly excluded in computing the net assets of the appellant. The assessee appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee, more entries in the books of account in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor and gift in such case will not be valid. [129B] (2) The assessee had made a valid gift of Rs 50, 000 on 1st January 1957 and credited the same in his personal account in his account in that year. It was held by the High court that there is no completed gifts of the principal amounts as there was acceptance of that gift by the donee. [130C] (3) The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [131D] (4) In the instant case, the assessee had paid Rs.50,00,000 in cash to his wife and a sum of money was available to that firm for physically giving her possession. It is not possible to say that the interest which were credited in the account of the minor donees by the firm which carried on money lending business also were fictitious. [132E] (5) The fact that the transaction was genuine and there was a receipt of Rs 25,000 from the father of the deceased did not constitute a valid transfer even though there was accepted gift by him would not make any difference to the question whether the amount was actually given or not. [133F G] (6) In view of the fact that there were no registered deed and as there were acceptance of the gift by donee, it resulted in a valid gifts, it could not be said that subsequently when money was transferred by further entries in his own account books, it had been received by him more than once. [134G] (7) The transfer was effected by debiting the assessee 's personal account and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K.

The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court and was posted as superintendent and legal remembrancer in March 1962. The High Court held that Shri B.K. Patro, district and sessions judges were not entitled to hold the posts in question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that the order of the High Court holding that those officers had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and Legal remembacker and member sales tax tribunal, respectively, on and after October 10, 1966 and (ii) that in view of the fact that the orders of the high court were made by the High Courts under article 233 of the Constitution, the High court was not competent to pass any order as it had no power to fill up some of the posts. HELD: The High court is not entitled, on principle, to hold that the High 'Court has power to make an order in respect of a particular post or class of posts. [629 D] Ranga Mahammad vs State of Orissa, ; , referred to. (i)(ii) In the course of the judgment this Court observed that after a judicial officer is posted to the cadre, it is for the High Judge to effect his transfers, the court below has come to the conclusion that as the posts of the law secretary and superintendent and other legal remaxies are included in the cadre the High. Court has power under article 235 to fill those posts by transfer of judicial officers.

The appellant, a co sharer, filed a suit for pre emption of the land in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and that the appellant was not entitled to pre empt the property. In appeal, the High Court held that there were no infringement or infringement of Articles 14 or 15 of the constitution. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The right of pre emment given to co sharers as well as to a tenant can be justified as they constitute a class by themselves. [127B] 2.1 In the present case, the suit land belonged to more than one co sharee and had not been sold jointly by all the co shar holders. It was not made by all co sharists jointly. The sale deed in question did not confer any right of preemption on the kinsfolk. [128C] 2(a) In the instant case, there is no justification for the classification contained m section 15 which conferred a right of Pre emption on the Kinsfrocy. [129D] 3.2 The expression 'other co shars ' in clause 'Fourthly ' of Section 15(1) of Act means only those co sharants who do not fail under clause 'First ' or 'Secondly ' or "Thirdly" of section 15(i)(b). In the case of tenants who hold under tenancy of the vendor or vendors the land or property sold or a part thereof, and are not made parties to the suit, they constitute an class by itself. [130D] 2 (a) The word 'other sharers ' in cl. (f) is used to serve as a residuary clause to ensure that, no co shareer is left out. It is not intended to confer any power on the court to grant pre emplo sion to the co co sharant or to a sub sharer. [131E] 3(b) The expression "other co share holders" in cl.(f) means only such co sharators who do so as are specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section15(1). [131F] 3 (c) The words 'other than one ' in Cl. (a), (b) and (d) of section 16(1), are wide enough to include all co co share owners who do no fail under cl. 'Firstly '. [132G] 3.(e) The meaning of the word 'any ' in section 15 (1)(b) is to be given a wider meaning than that of the words "other than a co co co sharing" and the word "other sharer" in Cl.(a) means also those co co shares holders who do nothing but not fail within cl. "Firstly" or "Secondly".

The father and his two sons executed a deed of compromise in respect of the entire subject matter of litigation. The father and the two sons, who were the sons of the father and their son, filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that they had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove that the amount was due and payable by them. In appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the trial court and directed the parties to maintain status quo till the disposal of the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the compromise deed dated 21.8.1987 was not binding on the alienees as they had no interest in the property prior to the compromise and therefore, the sale deeds were subsequent to 21.08.1987. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The alienees have no interest to account for mesne profits. They have only become owners of the properties from the date of sales which is more than three years ' old by now. [541C] 1.2 In view of the fact that there was a allegation of payment of Rs. 1 lakh to the alienee, which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too are covered by the sale deed in favour of the alienors to Seshiah who is present in Court, and counsel for the sons and after hearing the Advocate for the alieners, we make the following directions: 1) The compromise petition shall be accepted and in terms thereof the suit shall be disposed of and the terms of the compromise shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this Court for disposal of special leave petition.

The appellant company was a sick industrial company. The workmen of the Company got the benefit of sick leave granted to its employees under an award dated August 29, 1958 which contained a specific direction that it would be automatically provincialised when the benefits of the Employees ' State Insurance Scheme would become available to the workmen. The Tribunal made an award for 7 days sick leave on full pay and dearness allowance in 1958 subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply if the benefits were not fully paid. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award on the ground that it was violative of the provisions of section 49 of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the workmen of Jyoti Ltd., Baroda, had no right to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of continuous illness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sickness for which sickness benefit was last paid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in holding that benefits admissible under the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave were such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and the setting aside of the Tribunal 's award in that respect. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Tribunal has not given any reason for allowing the benefit to the appellant company. [84E] 2.1 The Tribunal had made an order for 7 day sick leave for 7th days in 1958, subject to condition that it should cease to be a sanctioned leave on the basis of the period of two days. It was not necessary in the circumstances of the case to award the benefit under the sick leave with retro spective effect from January 1, 1975 in the cases of Jyoti ltd., Baroda. [85F G] 2(a) The Tribunal has made an Award for 7 working days sick Leave on full wages and dearness allowances in 1958. It is not necessary that in the instant case, the Tribunal has given adequate reasons for allowing it work out to about half the average wage of a workman. [86G H; 86A B] 2 (b) The Industrial Court has made a finding that the sickness benefits would cease on full salary and dearness Allowance in 1958 and subject to conditions that the benefits would not cease to exist if the benefit was not fullypaid. [87F G; 87B C] 3(a). The Tribunal, therefore, made an interim award for seven days sick leaves on full emoluments during the period between January 1 1975 and January 1. 1975. [88G H] 3 (b). The Industrial Courts have to see whether the sickness is a bona fide one or not. If it is found that the disease was of such a nature as to require immediate medical attention, then the Tribunal should not in any case, give leave on complete emoluments for seven day sick Leave. [89F G].

The appellant was detained under section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1947. The grounds were served on him and he was informed that he had been supplied with copies of documents relied upon by the detaining authority. He was also given an opportunity to make a representation against the order of detention. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the grounds were vague or not at all, and that the alleged vagueness could not be said to have prejudiced his right to be furnished particulars under article 22(6) of the Constitution. Held, that the order was not vitiated by any violation of the constitutional rights guaranteed by article 22 (5). The grounds supplied in paragraph 12 of the petition were vague and not at least vague. The ground given in paragraph 13 of the grounds was not vague or even at all. The fact that the appellant had made a representation to the detaining Authority did not make him a proper representation. The right of the detenue to befurnished particulars under section 10 of the Act is subject to the limitation under article 21 of the constitution and the very information which has been supplied in paragraphs 12 and 13 of this petition must be taken to be different from the material relied upon. The power not to disclose facts considered against a person is subject only to the limitations provided by the Constitution and the Court cannot interfere with such an order unless it is shown that there was some other ground for interfering with the order. The question as to whether or not the grounds furnished are vague or at least in the nature of vague, does not arise for consideration in this case because the grounds supplied were open to the challenge of vagueness and the nature and activities imputed therein to the appellant.

The respondent was a member of the Indian Army and was dismissed from service. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r 14 of Army Rules 1954, which was intra vires the , was ultra legislative and void as it violated article 14 of Constitution. HELD : (i) Rule 14 of Indian Army Rules is a rule of substantive law and not of substantive nature. The rules are made in accordance with the provisions of the Act and such rules cannot be challenged on the grounds that they violate articles 14 or 16 of the constitution. [445 B] (ii) The words "subject to the provisions" occurring in r.14 make it clear that there should be rules, and subject to the provision of the Rules and regulations made thereunder the Central Government may dismiss or remove from service any person subject to this Act. [449 C D] (iii) Rule 15 is a general rule which does not prescribe any particular form of procedure for imposing an order of punishment. The words 'subject to provisions of this Act ' occurring in section 19 make it obligatory on the Central Govern ment to frame rules and regulations under the Act. The Rules do not contain any specific provision for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45. [453 D] In the instant case, the respondent was not considered unsatisfactory by the Central Govt. as required by r. 15 of the Defence Rules. [451 G] (iv) Rule 19 is a special rule and not a general one. The two sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive. They operate in different fields. The first section does not deal with any particular matter. It deals with the procedure for dealing with an appeal or revision application. The second section deals with cases where the order made by the disciplinary authority is set aside or quashed by a court of law. [454 E] (v) Rule 16 of Army Rule, 1954 provides that if the officer concerned was not tried by a Court martial, he shall be dismissed from the service. Rule 14 is such a rule which deals with removal from the Service of persons subject to Act. It does not say that the rules are ultra vires.

The appellant company was carrying on business as a dealer in tea. The respondent, who was the owner of the tea, was assessed to octroi duty under r. 21 of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1888. The appellant challenged the assessment on the ground that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r, 21. The High Court held that the Municipality had no power to levy a tax or fee and that the appellant was not entitled to any exemption from payment of octroi duty. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 22 of the Rules prescribes the procedure for levying tax or fees and is not confined to octroi duties only. The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. [218 E] (ii) The Standing committee was entitled, therefore, to deal in the appeal as it had failed to fix the octroi limit in accordance with law. Rule 22 does not prescribe any procedure for levy of tax or Fee and is headed "Appeal against levy of any tax orfee". It imposes a duty on the Municipality to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy, but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. [220 F] (iii) The appellant was entitled under r 21 to object only to these two matters, namely, (1) the tax or the fee imposed and the rate at which it is levied; (2) the period of sixty days of limitation commences from the date of the publication of the notice under r., 4, i.e., the notice following the decision of a Panchayat to levy any tax; (3) the time limit for the assessment of octroi and the rates at which the same is to be levied.

The appellant No. 1 was appointed as a Conciliation Officer under section 12(6) of the , and he was asked to appear before him on January 9, 1952, but he did not appear before the conciliation officer within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings were held in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the Conciliation Officer submitted his report on December 31, 1951, to the State Government. On January 9. 1952, the appellant No 1 was asked by the State to appear for a hearing before the Conciliation officer on January 10, 1952. The State Government passed an order under section 33 read with section 33(1) of that Act directing the appellant no. 1 not to proceed with the conciliation proceeding till June 2, 1952 and directed the appellant to pay Rs. 5 to the appellants. On December 31. 1952 the appellant filed a petition in the High Court for quashing the proceedings on the ground that the conciliation was illegal and that the Conciliation Officers were bound by the provisions Of section 12 of the . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice under section 34 of the was not properly served on the appellant and the proceedings were therefore illegal. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 12(1)(b) contemplates that the report should be made and the proceeding closed within a fortnight and if it is received by the Government, the report shall be submitted to the appropriate government. The provisions of section 20(2)(b), however, contemplate that the reports should be sent to the conciliation Officer within 14days and if proceedings are not closed but are carried on, as they were in the present case or if the Conciliation proceedings are held, as it was received by Government, then the report may be said to have been made and proceedings closed within 14 months. [738 B C] (ii) The Act provides for commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but the first sub section of section 12 contemplates that a report should he made and if the report is received before the appropriate Govern ment, the Government may be guilty of a breach of duty but in law the proceedings do not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20 (2)(a) of Act. The first sub sections of section 13 deal with what are called utility services and sub section 2 of that section provides for the submission of reports by conciliation officers within 14 weeks and if no settlement is reached, then it may be held that the enquiry was not completed within 14th day but only terminated as provided under section 17(6). [739 C D] (iii) The first subsection of section 18 contemplates that where a conciliation proceeding concluded before the commencement or when the report of the Conciliation Board is received in by the Appropriate Government, it shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement was reached, when the reports are received by it.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was involved in a criminal case. The order of detention was served on him on 22nd January, 1986 and the detenu was informed that the Advisory Board had confirmed the order of his detention. The petitioner challenged the said order by filing an application before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. [910C] 2. The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. It is not shown that either the prospect of immediate release of the petitioner or other factors which can justify the detention of a person in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles noted in the aforesaid decision. [0910D] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District magistrate Etah and others, , referred to. 2.1 The order is set aside. If A man is not in custody, and he is likely to be enlarged on bail, the powers of preventive remand should not ordinarily be exercised unless there are compelling reasons for doing so. [990D] 2:2 In the present case, when the actual order of the detention was passed and before the actual service of the Order of detention, the detenu had already surrendered for whatever reasons, therefore the order was not on proper consideration. It may be mentioned that in the affidavit of the District Magistrate it does not appear that either of the prospect or the question that the detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of the release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of detention. [991D E] Rameshwar figures as a result of the representation made on behalf of the State Government. The affidavit of District Magistrate is not supported by any material. It does not disclose that this factor or the questions that may be asked for the detenu to make an application under section 5(2)(b) of Act.

The respondent firm was a dealer in gold and silver. The appellant, a dealer under the Gold Control Act, 1968, issued a notice to the respondent firm for recovery of certain amounts due from it on account of sales tax payable by it. The respondent firm filed its return of income showing the total value of the gold and also claimed that the amount paid by it was not liable to be recovered from it as the appellant had failed to pay the same. The Income Tax Officer, after considering the explanation offered by the respondent, held that the respondent was entitled to a higher rate of tax on the gold in question. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax officer. In further appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High Court erred in striking down sec. 28 of the Gold (Control) Act, 1969 as it suffers from excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred on him under sec. 5(1) of the Act requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy and purposes of the statute in making his orders. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the enactment and the scheme of the Central Excise and Salt Act is to provide for prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the . Act. [954C] 2.1 The object and purpose of the legislation together with the necessity to ensure prevention of inter alia the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. In other words, the policy of the law and the Scheme provide sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [976D] 2(a) The object is to ensure speedy disposal of confiscated gold and to prevent misuse of such gold by the owner of the article. It does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. [977E] 2 (b) The scheme and the purpose for which the Act together with its necessity to provide sufficient safeguards to the administrator in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on it under section 5(2) of that Act requires the Administrator to have regard, inter alia, to the Policy and purposes for ensuring prevention of pre-empt of circumvenvention of other provisions contained in the Act.

The appellants were the owners of certain properties in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk, Tiruchirappalli District. The property involved in this case consisted of agricultural lands situated in Eramgudi Village and the lands involved in the suit were also cultivated by the appellants. The respondents 1 to 3 who were the tenants of the said properties filed a suit against the appellants for possession of the properties on the ground that they had acquired title by adverse possession, and that the appellants had not been holding the same as managers of the trust. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that in cases falling under article 134 B of the Constitution the transfer made by the manager of a Hindu endowment is challenged by his successor on the grounds (1) that the transfer was effected by the Manager without any authority; (2) that in case of adverse possession the possession of such transferee is adverse from the date of the transfer and (3) that he had been removed from office by other persons who were acting as de facto managers of a temple. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the title of the temple had not passed to the appellants on the basis that it belonged to them. [710 G] In the present case, the property involved was agricultural lands and the appellants were not holding the said lands as managers. They were not held by any person who was in management of the affairs of the Trust de facto. The fact that the alienor was still alive and so, the management had been taken over by other person who were in management, de facto, did not make him a manager of the property. [810 B C] Gnanasambanda vs Dossami Chettiar, I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant, a firm of three partners, was the sole licensee in respect of the Apsara Theatre. The licence was renewed by the District Magistrate, Jammu (8th defendant) for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsar Cinema. The appellant 's application for renewal of the licence was rejected by the licensing authority on the ground that the licence had been granted to him in his individual capacity and that he had been declared to be the sole proprietor in respect thereof. The District Magistrate held that the renewal of licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, Shri Ved Gupta who had been declaring to be a sole licensee. On appeal by the appellant, the State Government set aside the order of the licensing Authority and directed the Licensing Authority to renew the licence. The High Court held that since the licence in respect o the Aosar Cinema was granted by the district Magistrate in the sole name of Ved Gupta, he could not operate the cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the State government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licensing authorities had no jurisdiction under the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence and since it was only the licensee who was held responsible under the provisions of the Act and the Rules for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the Licence, he may be saved from any prosecution or other action under law in the capacity of licensee of theApsara Cinema. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The licensing authority had no power to suspend the licence which could not have been suspended by the order dated December 29, 1977. [578D] 2. The provisions of section 6 F of the , as amended by Act No. 8 of 1980, are mandatory and not directory. The Licensing Authority has no jurisdiction to suspend or cancel a licence. It is only the licensing officer who can suspend the licensee under section 6F of the . [579E] 3. The order passed by the Licensing authority directing suspension of the cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [579G] 4. The impugned order passed on December 29. 1977 is, therefore, void and in violation of the principles of natural justice. [580A B] 5. The respondent No. 2 has no power under the , or the rules for the suspension of a licence which entitled it to notice and hearing under the . Act before the licence is suspended. [581B C] 6. The writ petitioners have been given an opportunity to show cause against the order passed against them by the authority concerned. They have not been given any opportunity to defend their case. [584C D] 7. The State Government has no authority under the law or the rule making power to make such an order. It has no statutory duty to suspend and cancel a license which is granted by it in the public interest. [585D] 8. The right of the licensee to carry on the business of cinema is conferred only by section 6 H of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Section 6 F provides for suspension of licence. Section 7 A provides that no person shall carry on any business in or permit or permit to be carried on any work in connection with the exhibition of films in a public place unless he has been declared as the sole owner thereof. [586E] 9. The licensee is not entitled to have his licence renewed for exhibition at the time of his application for the licence and the rules made thereunder are not applicable to him. [587F] 10.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain mills in Bombay, were granted a lease of their mills for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. The appellants challenged the validity of the lease on the ground that it was not a lease granted by them to them as they had no authority under section 12 of the , and that the notice, Exhibit C, was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 10 of the Act. Held, that the provisions of section 12 were not applicable to the present case because the appellants had been given the right to cancel a lease in favour of the appellants. The notice, Exhibits C, and C, did not amount to any delegation of power by the Custodian to the Central Government. The notification dated December 13, 1951 issued under section 7 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, was valid as it applied only to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Government itself. The order Exhibit C was therefore illegal. The provisions of sections 12 and 13 of the were not attracted to the facts of the present appeal. The proceedings before the Custodian were not barred under section 11 of the Indian Act. The question whether a lease could be cancelled or varied in exercise of its powers under section 8(1) of the . was not raised in this Court. The effect of section 10 was that the Custodian had the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. The words "if any" in section 12 meant only those who were entitled to the same rights as those arising out of the leases, and not those arising from the lease. The word "transfer" in the section was used in a sense analogous to that of transfer of property. The expression "transfer of property" in sections 12, 13 and 14 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, did include a transfer by one person to another for consideration and it could not be said that the words "transfer or variation" in those sections were intended to cover transactions which had been entered into between the evacuee, and the evacuee. The fact that the property was transferred under section 2(1)(a) of that Act did not make any difference as regards the nature of the transaction. The Custodian could not cancel a transfer of lease granted to the appellants by himself and not on the evacuee; it was only when the property had been sold in favour by the appellants, that it could be said to have been transferred by the respondent to the evacuee or that the evacuee had no power under section 13 to cancel the agreement to sell. The right of the appellant to cancel an agreement to sale was therefore not affected by the provisions contained in sections 11 and 12 of Act.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for declaration that Surendrapal Singh, his father, had become major son of the respondent and that he was entitled to be declared as a minor. The trial court decreed the suit holding that Surendra Pal Singh (appellant herein) aged 12 years was a minor on 14th March 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalized by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. The appellant filed an appeal before the Board of Revenue which was dismissed. In the further revision application filed by the respondent, the Board held that Surendra pal Singh (Appellant herein) was born on 14 th March 1963, and was merely 13 years old when the Ceiling proceedings were finalised by the sub Divisional Officer. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that it was not correct to say that Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the Board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and control and the order of the Board could not be held proper with reference to section 9 of Land Revenue act. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Board noticed that there was no provision for separate unit in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional officer Hanumangarh, for de novo determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. [707C] 2. The State having by its order dated 14th April 1975 directed that the ceiling area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956 and not according to the new law i..e. in pursuance of the direction of the High Court, the SubDivisional Officer committed an error on the face of it. [807D] 3. The order of sub Divisional officer dated 14 th April 1975 was set aside by the Board. The case was remitted to Sub Divn. Officer Hanumanganagar for devo determination of his calling area. The Sub Divisional Officers were directed to dispose of the case within a period of three months from the date of receipt of this order. [607E] 4. The sub Divisional Officers have no power to set aside an ex parte order passed by the subordinate authorities and, therefore the Board has no jurisdiction to set it aside. [508F] 5. The question whether Section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the State Government over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. The power of superintendence under section 222 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not subject to any other provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code. It is clear from the language of section 221 of the Cr. P.C., that the Boards have general powers of control over all revenue courts. In this case, the High Courts have by their order dated 13th April, 1975 directed the Sub Divi sion Officer to dispose off the ceiling areas for the appellant in law. The District Revenue Officer has also by his order dated 6th September, 1976 directed that he should dispose of all the cases within a specified time.

The first respondent, the Chief Secretary of the State Government, issued a notification dated January 21, 1973 under section 3(1) of the , declaring that the employees of the appellant company were entitled to the benefit of the orders made by the Central Government on the basis of recommendations of the Justice Palekar. The first respondent filed an application before the Central Govern ment for permission to compound the offences punishable under sections 7 and 8 of the . The Central Government granted permission to the first respondent to compound certain offences punishable with imprisonment for a period of one year. The appellant company challenged the said order by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on March 22, 1983. In the appeal before this Court it was contended that the law reports published by the Ist respondent were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by Central Government under section 2(b) of Act was unsustainable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.
