The law reports which are being published by a first respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court of India and of the High Courts in India which are supplied to it by its agents appointed at New Delhi and other places where High Courts are situated. They are binding on all the courts throughout India. [775B] 2. The Act is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of employees of a newspaper establishment and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the Act the one which advances the object of the statute and is in favour of the employees for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [779C] 3. The expression 'newspaper ' as defined by section 2 (b) means "any printing press, or any other newspaper, or magazine containing news which members of the public ordinarily read in order to get reports of previous events, comments on them etc. [781D E] 4. The word 'new ' is defined in section 2 of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 as meaning "any work relating to or connected with any newspaper establishment". It is a well settled principle that a statute has to specify the particular subject matter which is the subject matter of the legislation. [780E F] 5. The definition of 'new' in the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 is wide enough to include not merely 'public news ' but also `comments on public news '. It is clear from the definition of the expression `newspapers ' that the expression "news paper" as defined under the Act includes not only `public news ` but also 'comments in any newspaper, and therefore, even if a particular kind of publication is made by a person who has no connection with the affairs of the newspaper establishment, it would be difficult to agree with the submission that the word `new ' should be construed as meaning `public newspaper '. [783E F; 776A B] 6. The fact that the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant on the ground that he was a licensee and also incidentally the question whether the appellant was a tenant or not. The appellant contended that he had been in occupation of the premises under a subsisting agreement for licence, and therefore, the Court of Small Causes Bombay had jurisdiction to deal with the eviction petition. The respondent denied that he is a licensee or a tenant and further contended that the appellant had failed to prove that he has been a licensee. The Small Cause Court held that the respondent was a direct tenant and not a tenant. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court set aside the finding of the Small Causes Court and restored the order of eviction passed against the appellant. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the respondent that there was sub tenancy by the appellant in favour of the Respondent as a monthly tenant of the business with the articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The facts and circumstances of the case are clearly established beyond doubt that the parties had entered into an agreement for leave and licence and the appellant licensor was a lessee and not merely a licensee but also incidentally, the question as to whether he was in occupation or not is a matter which has to be determined by considering all relevant factors. [231B] 2. The fact that the landlord had entered with the respondent on the one hand and the tenant had entered on the other does not make any difference. It is only when the landlord has entered into a contract with the tenant that he can terminate the agreement earlier than the tenant. In such a case, the landlord cannot be said to have been a sub tenant. [232C] 3. The question whether a licensee is a tenant is essentially one of fact and depends upon the facts and circumstance of each case. It has to depend on the facts of each particular case. [233D] 4. In the instant case, it was not a licence but a lease. good deal of submission was made before the Court that if it was a lease and not an agreement, then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the Court had to jurisdiction, and there was no estoppel. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. & others vs Shri Vishwa Nath & 5 others, [1987] 2 scale 27, held inapplicable.

The appellant was a Ruler of the erstwhile State of Rajasthan. He was assessed to income tax on the income derived from the business carried on by him in the State of Jaipur. The appellant claimed that the liability of the former Ruler to refund the amount of tax collected in advance for no export was not enforceable against the latter. The claim was rejected by the Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the appellant had been recognised by the new sovereign and relied on the continuance of the laws in the covenanting State till they were repealed or altered, recognised that it was liable in the same way as would have been the merging State if there was any liability on the merged State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The appellant had not been recognised under the agreement with the Ruler of Rajasthan and his claim for refund of tax was rightly rejected by him. [179 D] (ii) The agreement was not a law. It was not an act of State. The agreement did not confer any right on the company as against the new State. [180 E] (iii) The liability of a former Ruler of Jaipur to refund, the amount paid in advance, for no exports was made, that is, it emerged from the merger of the territory and there was no recognition by the old sovereign of the existing rights of the residents of those territories. [181 F G] (iv) The new State continued all the old laws till they came into force. There was always recognition by a new sovereign of its existing rights in the territory. It follows therefore that there was always recognised by new sovereign as well as reliance on continuance of laws and article VI of the Covenant in that connection.

The appellant was a trader in cotton. He had a licence to sell the goods to the respondent for the purpose of sale. The respondent purchased the goods from the appellant and sold them to the appellant. The appellant 's contention that the sales were not liable to tax under section 14 of the Act, was rejected by the Sales Tax Officer. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the appellant had only two fundamental rights: (1) that the purchase of cotton was a trade allowance; and (2) that it was not covered either by section 14 or by bye laws framed thereunder as section 14 prohibited the deduction of trade allowance and did not operate upon any other payments made which were not trade allowances. The High Court, on reference, held that though the appellant was carrying on business in cotton, no licence to purchase or sell such a commercial crop could be granted or renewed in respect of any place situated within the State. On further appeal by special leave, Held: (i) that under section 19(1)(a) of the , the State Government has to establish a market committee for every notified area and it is not necessary that the allowance should be paid to the members of the Market Committee or the members who are not members of any other Market Committee. The word 'mahimai ' in section 14 means a person holding a licence for selling cotton but does not include a person who has a licence under the Act to sell goods. The words "any place situated outside such area" in section 19 (1)(b) mean a place which is situated within such area and includes a place where it is situate within such distance of the market as may from time to time be fixed by the State Govt. [108 B C] (ii) that by reason of the notification they are not prevented from doing their business, for they can still utilise it for commodities other than the notified crops. The fact that the appellants were carrying on trade or business and the respondent was entitled to the benefit of section 14 does not affect the right of the appellant to carry on his business. The object of the section is to provide for better regulation of the business in the State, and the object of this provision is to ensure that the business carried on by a trader is not affected thereby. (iii) that section 19 of the is bad because it does not operate as a bar against the levy of tax on the purchase or sale of any notified agricultural produce. The Act does not provide for the levy, but only provides for the imposition of a tax on transactions in respect o the commercial crops. It does not make any distinction between a transaction which is outside the purview of section 19 and a transaction in respect which the seller may purport to sell one maund of cotton but in fact deduct a small part of it, retain that part for himself or give it to C; or both A and B may fix the price of the commodity purchased at Rs. 1/ per quintal. The question whether the appellant is a trader or not has to be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. (iv) that in view of the fact that there was no agreement between the parties, the respondent could not claim any benefit under section 15 of the .

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the sentence but on appeal by the State, the appellant contended that the death sentences were excessive and that the High Court should not have reduced the sentence of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia. Held, that the conviction was justified under section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the High Courts had no power to reduce the sentence. The fact that the appellant was acquitted by the High court did not justify an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. The facts disclosed do not warrant an inference that there was common intention between the accused and the deceased. The circumstances established clearly showed that the accused had committed the murder and the injury on the throat is ascribed to him in the charge. The appellant was guilty of murder under section 304 Part I, Indian Penal code and sentenced for life imprisonment. The sentence of the High. Court was confirmed by the Supreme Court. The appeal must be dismissed. The conviction of the appellant under section 201 of the Penal Code was justified on the evidence. The case of the prosecution was that the deceased had been murdered with his stick and assigns no particular blow to the other two accused. The injuries on the face were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. There was no evidence to show that the assailants were responsible for the murder. The evidence showed that there were several persons who were present at the scene of the crime but none was examined by the prosecution as to who had assaulted the deceased and who had not appealed, with sticks.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service but on 4.9.1965 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating position and was re spondent No. 1. The petitioner challenged his reversion by a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution contending that he had attained the age of 55 years on 10.2.1972 and, therefore, on the date of order he had completed the age Of 54 years. The High Court held that the petitioner had attained 60 years on the said date when he was compulsorily retired. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The ratio of the decision in Tahiliani 's case is not applicable to the facts of this case as the petitioner has not attained the 55 years age on 10th2 1972 and, hence, on that date he had reached the age 55 years. [690B] 2.1 In the instant case, the petitioner was promoted as officiating Assistant Engineer which is a Class II post on 25.5.1971 and on 4 9 1965 he was reduced to the rank of Assistant Engineers in officiating capacity. The promotion order dated 3.8.1976 was issued by the Government under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. [643C D] 2:2. In the present case, there is no warrant for the conclusion that officiating Government servants in Class II or Class II service or post are outside the purview of sub clause (i). The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(J)(i). [691C D, H] 2I2 In the case of Tahiliami 's Case, the Court held: "The ratio of this decision is not correct and sub clause(i) has to be confined to service or posts held on substantive basis. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 (j)(ii) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii). [643D E] 2l2 In this case, it was not disputed that a person who is in Class III or Class I Service or post has been compulsorily retired under Fundamental Rule56(j). The fact that the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sation is exercised does not make any difference. [641D E; 642A] 3:3.

The respondent Corporation issued a cheque for Rs. 1,00,000/ to the appellant Corporation in respect of the policy taken by it from the deceased. The cheque was encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the account towards premium payable by the deceased on the date of the receipt of the balance towards premium. The respondent Corporation thereupon issued a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the appellants, calling upon them to pay the amount. The appellants resisted the claim contending that the proposal was not accepted and as such there was no concluded insurance contract between the deceased and the Corporation. The trial court held that the cheque was not received by the Corporation completely on 11th January, 1961 but it was also appropriated by it in its accounts and the said premium amount was received by it without any demur or qualification and that the acceptance of the proposal did not alter the position as under the rules the payment of the first premium could never amount to the acceptance. The High Court held that there was a concluded contract of insurance between the respondent Corporation and the deceased, and that there had been no concluded contract between them. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the deceased was not entitled to any benefit under the policy because he was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment would amount to acceptance of a proposal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that there is no concluded agreement between the parties does not alter its position as per rules. [354B] 2.1 The High court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there could be a concluded policy of insurance. The contract of Insurance is complete by offer and acceptance. It is not necessary for the Corporation to accept the proposal when it is accepted. In the instant case, the proposal must be accepted by the Divisional Manager and that alone could give rise to a valid contract of policy of Insurance which never happened in this case. [355C D] 2:2 The High Courts were in error on the ground that having regard to the conduct of the parties, there was concluded contract. There is no evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. [356D E] 3.1 In the present case, there is a concluded agreement of insurance and the acceptance thereof by the respondent was not only accepted but it also accepted the proposal. The acceptance of proposal was therefore not established. [358F G] 2 2.3 The HighCourt was in wrong in coming into the conclusion on the basis of the evidence that there were no concluded contracts of insurance, and the High Court was in a wrong error in reaching the conclusion. [359G] 3:4. In view of the clear position in law about acceptance of insurance proposal and the evidence on record in this regard, it is not possible to come to the finding that there has been a concluded contracts. The finding of the High court that there did not have any concluded contract is correct.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, filed a writ petition in the High Court for clarification of the judgment dated 4th November, 1988. The High Court held that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of goods manufactured by the processor plus the value or deemed price at which the processed goods would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the valuation of the processing machine would be a value of Rs.30, being the value for the grey cloth plus the cost of the job work done plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses, what was required to include the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The valuation of processing machine is a concept of a price for the purpose of assessment of excise duty. It is not necessary to include a trader 'in respect of the grey fabric or fabric plus the price of the process done plus the manufacturing profit. [346C] 1.2 The valuation is made on the basis of the price at the factory gate or deemed to be the price under section 4(1)(a) of the Act. The price at that time was the price for which the processing machinery would leave it and the person authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili ty under the Act and the rules made thereunder. [347C] 2.3 The valuation in respect of processed fabric is a method of computation of the value, and the Rules made thereunder are not applicable to the facts of this case. [348D] 2(a) The valuation has been made on a price basis for the processing machines. It was not necessary that the trader should have any other subsequent profit or expenses. [349F] 3.1 In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value is Rs.20 and the value in respect o o o of job work performed plus manufacturing profits and manufacturing cost, whatev er these may be, which will either be included in the price or deemed t o be the prices at the Factory gate for the processed fabrics. [350G] 3(b) The Valuation Rules made under section 17 of the are not attracted to the case of the respondent assessee.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a head clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 33 of the Amending Act provided for conditions of service of the Government servants allotted to the Panchayat Samitis, and until they are absorbed in the Government service or retire in such manner as may be prescribed. By a notification dated April 1, 1975, the Government of Haryana notified absorption of the appellant as a clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 the appellant was confirmed as a Sub Clerk. On April 1.1975 he was confirmed with effect from April 1 1974. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his absorption on a lower post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had no right to be considered for promotion and that the Panchayat Samities were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that by reason of section 14(4) of the Act the appellant is entitled to continue in the service of a Head clerk even though he was working as a sub Clerk in the Loharam Panchayat Samiti. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appel lant to the post of Head Clerk being without the authority of law, the government was not bound to absorb him in the post. He is appointed lawfully to the same terms and conditions on which he was employed by the panchayat Samiti until he was absorbed in Government service. [707D] 2. The fact that the appell lant was promoted to a lower grade, his appointment as Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. [077E] 3. The right to appointment is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant has been entitled to be promoted but, whether the Panchayat samities had the right to appoint him to the posts of Head Clerks on the date on which it purported to do so. [807F] 4. The mere fact that a person was promoted on an Ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed lawfully lo the post, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the amendment Act came into effect.

The appellant was the Mahant of Math Sauna. He died in 1917 leaving behind his widow, two sons and four daughters. The property was purchased by the appellant from the personal and separate funds received by him from his father Shivshanker Yati. The properties were sold to the appellant 's brother Shivshankar Yati on November 12, 1892. The appellant filed a suit claiming that he was the chela of Mahant Shivs Shankar Yati and that he had been in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiva Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of the Math Saunkar, and that the Amauli properties were purchased by him for Rs. 40,000 forming part of a fund left behind by his predecessor Shivsarayan Yati, and therefore he was entitled as Sarbarkar to all the properties recorded in the deity Mahadeo Ji or in the name of Mahant Ram Shankar Yatak. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant was not an ordinary Hindu Mahant of a Math Saiva and that it could not be said that he belonged to the Math or the deity. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The fund from which the Amaulik Yati executed a will in 1956, was constituted the personal property of Mahant Shiva Shankar YATI. He was granted a succession certificate by the District Judge, Ghazipur in respect of the two fixed deposits made by him in the Bank of Bengal. Mahant Shivram Yati died in 1921 and he was succeeded by his heirs. The fact that Sadasiv Yati had executed a trust deed in 1956 does not make any difference to the question whether the fund was the personal or separate property of the Mahant. [666 D E] (2) The funds from which a Amauli property was acquired constituted the Hindu Religious Income Tax Act 1948, and the Amaulia properties were described by Mahant Shivashankar Yatkya as properties of the institution. The income from these properties was therefore assessable to tax. [663 F G] (3) The appellant ' s claim that he could not claim exemption from the levy was made. The claim was not accepted by the assessing authority and that was a claim for exemption from payment of the levy. [664 A B] (4) The property from which Amauli income was acquired was not personal property. The burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim is discharged by the party claiming exemption from tax. In the present case, the appellant had also inherited the personal properties of Shivsary Yati from time to time and therefore a claim to exemption from levy was rightly made. [662 B C] (5) The Amauli assets constituted the joint family property of which the appellant claimed exemption from taxation. The fund was purchased in 1920 by the father Shivram Yadav, who in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amariar. He had also acquired the personal right to possess and acquire personal property and were entitled to possess, enjoy and acquire any personal property as he was his own. [661 D E; 662 A B]. (6) The income tax authorities have rightly held that the fund from whom the Amauri properties were acquired constituted a personal property within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act.

The appellants were allotted to the respondents ' land in the village of Raikot in 1949. The respondents applied for a quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 5 1/4 units of land in their favour on the ground that they had been granted quasi permanent allotments in the same village named Humbran in the said village. The Deputy Custodian General rejected the application holding that the appellants were not entitled to quasi permanent allocation of 40 standard acres, and that the notification issued under section 12(1) of the Act was invalid as it violated article 14 of the Constitution. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the respondents had no right to hold any land in excess of the permissible area under section 8 of the , and the notification was not invalid on the grounds that the order of the Deputy Custodian was without jurisdiction. The notification issued thereunder was valid and could not be challenged as being violative of article 14 Of the Constitution; it was not necessary for the respondents to have filed a suit in the civil court against the appellants. The fact that subsequent to the issue of the notification under section 13(1), the property would cease to be evacuee property, the aforesaid powers of the Custodian were in conflict with those conferred by section 19 of the 1954 Act on a managing officer or managing corporation constituted under that Act. The power of the custodian under section 19 was not confined only to the property which had been allotted but had also to be taken into account for determining whether it was evacuee property. The order of allotment made under section 11(1)(a) of this Act was valid, and could be challenged by a person who had no title to the land in question.

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Inspectress of girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) and the advertisement was published on May 5, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examination was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the computation of marks, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examination. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Service Com mission in cancelling the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that the written test was not conducted by the Commission. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examinations and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exams from the interview, there is no justification to cancel the written parts of the selection examina tion. [126E] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a new interview of the two Scheduled Caste candidates on that basis. There was no reason for cancelling of the written Part of the Recruitment Examination. On the other hand, the situation could be suitably met by set aside the litigation could have be avoided. [127F] 1:3 When no defects were pointed out, in regard t he written examination and the exclusive selection process, there were no justification ful lished for cancelling a written part. The State Public Service commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not hap to suffer; public time would not be wasted in requiring re doing of what had once been done and the litigation can have been avoided. It is, therefore, directed that the order of the Commission cancelling the whole recruitment examination shall stand vacated.

The appellant, who was the original plaintiff, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the Dera and properties attached to it. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant as the lawfully appointed mahant was entitled to manage the properties of the deceased. The High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Das died and the appeal could be continued under Q. 10(1) in other cases of an assignment, creation or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the properties belonged to the D.era, he was not entitled to recover possession of those properties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have erred in holding that after death of the defendant, Shia Das, as his Chela, was a legal representative of the estate of the late father of Som Das. [488B] 1.2 In other cases, of an assignor, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. It was, however, contended on their behalf that there was no devolution of interest in the subject matter of the suit on the death or of any other reasons. The suit was filed on the basis that the plaintiff as the legally appointed mahants had no right to recover the property of theDera. [489C D] 1:3.1 In the instant case, the appellant was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahant of the respondent within the time prescribed by law. The subject matter was the interest of the third parties and it devolved upon the appellant by virtue of his election as mahants. [490C D; 491A] 1 2.2 The suit is for possession and management of the properties attached thereto by the appellant purporting to be the de facto mahant against Som Dass as de jure mahant. The property belonging to the third party was the subject of a partition between the two parties. The appellant was suing in his own capacity as maardar of the said Dera. He claimed that he was lawfully appointed as maistry and that the suit was not maintainable. [493C E] 1 3.3 In the present case, there is no doubt that the property belonged to Dera but it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Dass was elected to be his mahant and the appellant had no locus standi to institute the appeal. The fact that it was on his death that Shiaam Dass had been elected as mahtkar of the dera, could make no difference when we are dealing with the question whether the interest in Dera took place as an mahant or otherwise. [495C E; 491D] 1 4.1 It is difficult to believe that the respondent was a person interested in the suit property and he had no title to it at all. The question of devolution of the interest by the respondent on the deceased father of the first appellant was not raised before the High Court. [595G H; 491B] 2.3 The High court should have granted leave to the appel lant to prosecute the appeal and thereafter dismissed the appeal in limine. [500C D].

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer, and they were confirmed on October 29, 1979. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated October 29.1979 amending the Fundamental Rules by adding the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said amendment in the High Court. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the proviso to Rule 2(1) of the Fundamental Rule, which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be amended so as to empower the Government to alter those conditions to their prejudice and that the decision of the Government is bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of the age. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The amendment of February 17, 1983 to the Fundamental rules was made by the Government of India in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso under Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. [142E] 2.1 The object of the amendment is to reduce the age and to enable the Government servants to improve their conditions on the eve of retirement. It is not a case where the Government has power to alter or amend the conditions of services. The proviso to this rule is only an enabling provision which enables the Government servant to alter the conditions to his prejudice and, in any event, they cannot be substituted for the original condition of service.

The appellant, a dealer in goods, was carrying on business as dealers in goods. The Sales Tax Officer held that the goods were not liable to purchase tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution and therefore the sales were exempt from tax under section 8(b). The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that there was no evidence to show that the sale was effected by a registered dealer. The Appellate Tribunal held that it was not necessary for the assessee to prove that the sales had been effected by him or by a person to whom he sold the goods. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10(b) were intended to be used only in the course of export and not in the case of a registered person who has given such certificate under section 7(a). The words " any person " are meant for being brought on board the ship and so the sale is effected by the person to which he has sold the property. The word " registered dealer" in section 8 (b) means a registered dealers to whom the certificate has been issued under section 10. The words 'any person ' in section 9(b), however, are not intended to include a registered firm or a firm. The expression " any other person" in the section is used in the sense of a person who is not a registered partner and it is not necessary that he should be a registered proprietor. The fact that the word "registered dealer" is used does not mean that the person who carries on business must be a dealer. In the present case, the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board them. The sales were therefore exempt from taxation under article 366(1) (b).

The appellant, who was a married woman, filed an application under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code for a monthly allowance for maintenance. The Magistrate held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 400/ for her minor child. The High Court dismissed the petition in limine. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Courts below had failed to appreciate the true scope of section 125(4) (b) of the Code, which reads: "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. The question whether the applicant was a wife is a matter for determination in this appeal. If the answer to this question is in the affirmative, the Court will have jurisdiction to decide the question on its own merits. " Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts had failed in appreciating the true import of section 127(3) (a). The object of the payment under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties was to obviate destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [81 F] 2.2 In the instant case, the appellant had forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree of 1962 resolved all disputes and settled all claims then available but there was no mutual consent to live separately. The Court below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b). The High court had failed on this ground. [82 F] 3.1 In the present case, it is clear that the parties entered into a contract to adjust their then mutual rights. No settlement of claims which does not have the special statutory right of divorce can operate to negate that claim. Payment of mehar money as a customary discharge is within the cognisance of that provision. [83 F] 4.2 The HighCourt had failed and erred in ignoring the true effect of section 126(3)(b) which reads "if any in statutory interpretation belongs to the ill used wife and the derelict divorcee. he shall have no right to claim under section 127 (3)(a). " [84 C D] 5.1 Section 127(4)(b), which is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties, does not require that the divorced wife should be given a reasonable relation to the object and is a capitalised substitute for the order under section 126. [84 E] 5 2.3 The High courts had failed, in appreciating that the scope of Section 125(1) was manifestly to recognised the substitute ' maintenance arrangement ' by lump sums payment organised with the social obligation to maintain itself. The whole scheme of section127(3), is manifestly clear and unambiguous and the husband liberated.

The appellant was a dealer in the business of sale and purchase of rice. The Collector of the district after considering the representation made by him, cancelled the bid of the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal before the Collector. The same was dismissed on the ground that there was no requirement for giving any prior notice as required under section 5(2) of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1948. The order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector and the letter dated 25th March 1988, states as follows: "The Collector of District Samastipur has been informed by the Collector that the appellant is not interested in any future business of the dealer. Hence the appeal filed by the appellant be dismissed." The Collector rejected the appeal on the view that there is no requirement specifically of giving any notice under section 6(2). The order passed by the collector was under challenge before the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appel lant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. [868C] 1.2 In the instant case, the last portion was not affected by any order passed under section 3(3) of Bihar Sales tax Act, 1947. The respondent is right. But it is an implied principle of natural justice that parties affected by a order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order.

The appellant LIC, a public limited company, was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of iron and steel products. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant LIC on the ground that the premises were let out to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect thereof. The Rent Controller held that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit P 1 had also been conveyed to the appellant, but that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal holding that the building on the property leased under the exhibit P1 had also become an asset of the LIC. In second appeal before the High Court, the appellant contended that since the subject matter of the lease under exhibitP 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no jurisdic tion to determine the fair rent. The High Court held that since there was relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties, it could not be said that the Rent Control Act was applicable to the premises leased under exhibits P1 and P2. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the appellant is a tenant in or landlord of the building and the question whether he is a landlord within the purview of section 4(4) of Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & Rent Control ) Act, 1961 is only a determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. If the Civil Court in this case had come to the conclusion that there was a relationship of a landlord and a tenant and that he was entitled thereto, for such a suit would be barred by section 12(4). [570C D] 1.2 The question on which the jurisdiction of the civil court is excluded is only the determination as regards the fair and standard rent of the premises and not the determination of the fair Rent of the property. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the landlord and the tenant, the rent controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the fair rents are and then fades out of the picture. In the instant case, on a proper construction of the Rent control Act, the question onwhich the jurisdiction is excluded was only the determining as to whether the applicant is a 'tenant ' or the land is not ryoti land; in the instant cases it was the latter and such decision on the nature or character of the land has been given a finality under section 64 C which cannot be ques tioned in a court of law. [570D E] 1:3. The question as to principle, whether there is relationship of 'landlord and tenant and whether the landlord is entitled thereto is only that determination as an order that is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent controller under the Act. [571E F] 1 4. The word 'landlord ' in section 2 (1)(a) of Act means a person who holds land for his own use or for any other purpose. It is not necessary that the landlord must be a tenant or a tenant, but it is sufficient if he has acquired the right to occupy the land by himself. [572F] 5. The words 'landlord " in section 4 (4) are clear and unambiguous. The expression 'landlord" in section 3(1) of that Act means the person who has been let out for a period of five years or more, and not any other person. In view of this definition, it is not possible to hold that the word 'tenant " in Section 4 (3) is wide enough to include a landlord who has acquired a right to evict his tenant. [573F G] 6.

The petitioner was a respondent who had not appeared before the Central Government and, therefore, could not be heard by the Court. The Central Government issued an order dated April 1, 1966 directing that the list of officers on an integrated seniority list should be prepared in accordance with the rules governing seniority. The petitioner challenged the said order by filing writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution contending that he was entitled to a representation against the final list and that the same had been rejected by the Central Govern ment. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioner was not heard after the final lists were prepared. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of the Central Govt. dismissing the writ petition was premature as the final seniority list of the officers on a integrated seniority had been prepared and published in accordance therewith. HELD: (i) The petitioner 's claim for a right to have a say against the provisional list cannot be sustained. [828 B] (ii) The order of a few lines by which the petitioner ' s claim was disposed of by the High Court on the ground that he had been given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. [827 C D] (iii) The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by them before the final select list was prepared. [826 E F] (iv) The High Courts have been vested with the power to issue directions for the purpose of determining the seniority of the persons who are likely to be affected by the proposed assignment of a particular place. If that is established, the decision of the authorities concerned will have to stand. If a particular decision is mala fide or arrived at on totally irrelevant and extraneous consideration, such a decision can be interfered with by Courts.

The petitioners are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of sub para (10) of para 218 of Import & Export Policy 1978 79, which lays down that Additional licences issued to Export Houses/Trading Houses prior to April 1, 1988 or issued after April 1.1988, on exports made during 1986 87 or earlier periods shall not be eligible for the flexibilities in the import of items of raw materials, components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and Part A, and items of non OGL capital goods (other than those covered by appendices 1 to 4) available under the revised Policy. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that sub para(10) was not applicable to the petitioners as they were granted Additional licences on or after April 01, 1988 and the Export Houses who would be granted Additional Licences on or before April 1., 1988 in as much as the Export House which were issued Additional licences under the Import & Exports Policy 197879 had been denied the facilities which have been given to Export House who were issued additional licences on the basis of exports made by them during the period 1977 78. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners challenging the constitutional validity of Sub para (9) of Para 218 of the Import and Export Policy, 1978 79 were dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court. In the appeals to this Court it was contended that sub paras (10), (11) and (12) of the said para are not applicable in the present case as the conditions of eligibility for grant of Additional licences and the value of such additional licence are quite different from those contained in the Import Policy 1978 80, and that under Import & export policy 1978 79 the basis for grant or extension of the Additional Licences is the f.o.b. value of the exports made in 1977 78 whereas under Import and Exports Policy 1988 91, Additional licences were to be given on the strength of not foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made and the values of such Additional licences are only 10 to 12% of the net foreign exchange earning. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of sub paras(10),(11) & (12), are not attracted in the instant case as they relate to the period of validity of the additional licence under Import Policy, 1979 79. [236B] 2.1 Under the Import Control Policy 1978 81, Additional Licences were to remain valid for a period of 12 months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. The period of renewal of Additional Licences was not extended by six months as per the Import policy 1978 80. [237C D] 2(a) The petitioners who are granted Additional Licence under the import & Export policy 197879 have to be treated at par with Export Houses which have already expired during that period and since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para.(4) of 246 para 215 in respect of Additional licence granted to Export houses under the Imports & Exports (Control) Act, 1985, the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation.

The appellant, a manufacturer of bulk drugs and medicines, was manufacturing bulk drugs. The goods were delivered to the buyers in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer. The packing was not returnable to the buyer and the packing was only of durable nature and returnable by him. The appellant sold these goods to the customers who were carrying on business as dealers in bulk drugs, and the price was included in the assessable value. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal the goods were deliver ed from the factory in packed conditions and the container was not delivered by the buyers to the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that since the Act provides for only one exception to this measure, namely, non inclusion of the cost of packing where the packing is durable in nature and is returnable by a buyer to the manufacturer, in all other cases the cost should be included in its assessable value even when the packing has been supplied by the assessee and not the manufacturer. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression 'assessable value ' as interpreted in section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act is to provide for excise duty with reference to value of the excisable goods, while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate is the degree of packing. [975C D] 1.2 The object of the charging provision is to fix the assessable values and not to determine the assessable valuation. The cost of the packing would have to be included within the assessable price if necessary, by addition to the sale price except where the packed is of a durable character and is produced by the manufacturer to the factory. [977F G] 1:3 In the instant case, the appellant sold the goods to customers who are carrying on their business as wholesale dealers in the packed condition. The "cost of packing" contemplated in section 3(4) of that Act for determining the assessablevalue under section 4 (4)(a) is only the "cost ' of such packing which is returnable to manufacturer. [978F G; 975A] 1 Whether the cost is includible in the value of excisable goods is a question of fact depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. The object, purpose and purpose for the levy are not to be determined by addition thereto but only where the sale is of durability and returnable to a manufacturer. In this view of the matter, the cost cannot be included.

The appellant temple was a private temple. The temple was dedicated for the worship of a family idol. The deity installed in the temple was Shri Vithal Rukhamai. The appellant claimed that the temple had always been treated as trust property even by the Adhikari saints and the Adhikaris or the disciples who succeeded one after the other were not owners but trustees of the property. The High Court held that the properties were public religious endowments, and not a private property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was absolutely no evidence in this case about dedication to the public or public user of the temple as a matter of right. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The deity is a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act. [557B] (2) The properties in question were granted not in favour of an idol but in favour one Daryao Gir who was maintaining a temple and to his heirs in perpetuity. The property had always be treated as a trust property, even by a person who was maintained by the owner or the trustees of a property. [525C] (3) The temple is a private one and it is not a public religious endowment. It is a well known fact that the deity installed therein is a charitable institution. The properties are public religious trusts. The idol is a religious trust within section 2 (13) and its endowments are public trusts. [ 525D E] (4) The High Courts have rightly held that there is absolutely no material to show that the appellant was ever treated as an idol or temple. [ 526F G] (5) The fact that a temple is dedicated for worship of the family idol, it is a matter which can be determined by the Court in the absence of any evidence in the long history of the Sansthan to warrant that it had any appearance of or that it was ever treating as a public endowment. [506F G; 527A] (6) The appellant has not been able to show any material to justify that the property is a trust. It was never treated as private property and it never came into existence. [504E F] (7) The evidence of the deity shows that the idol installed in a temple was intended by the Founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public. [500F G]. (8) The Court will have to resolve the controversy about the character of the trust on documentary evidence, if any, lead to the inescapable conclusion that the character or devolution of the properties on documentary evidences is all important elements in determination of the question whether a property is private or public religious Endowment. [5000E] (9) The finding of the High Court that the respondent was not entitled to worship at the shrine of the Temple as a result of dedication to it by the appellant temple is correct and does not call for any interference.

The appellant was arrested and detained in execution of a warrant issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The respondent filed an application for release of his property on the ground that section 46(2) of the Act had been contravened by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 16(2), which provided for two different and alternative methods of recovery of arrears of land revenue, was violative of article 21 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that section 17 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was ultra vires article 14 of the constitution; (2) that the income tax being a subject with respect to which the Union alone may make law and the recovery of it being the Union responsibility, the machinery for the recovery thereof should be framed on a uniform all India basis for to the Union all defaulters who may not pay up the Union demand are similarly situated; and (3) that under section 46 (2), the Collector, on receipt of a certificate from the Income tax Officer, has to proceed to recover from such defaulter the amount specified therein as if it were an arrear of land Revenue. HELD: (i) The provisions of all the State laws are not inconsistent with article 21 and therefore they must be read into section 46. [157 D] (ii) Section 46(1) provides for two distinct and alternative modes of recovery, namely, (a) by way of attachment of property or sale of any movable property; (b) by attachment of the property of any person; and, (c) by a process of attachment and sale. The section does not provide that the Collector should proceed to recovering from the defaulting assessee the amount mentioned therein as arrears of revenue.

The appellants were the employees of the Bombay Port Trust. The respondents to this appeal are the trustees of the Port of Bombay. They were appointed by the Central Government under section 10(2) of the , as the "inclusive of one or more specified intervals" in sub rules (1) and (2) Of r. 24 of the Rules. The appellants were employed by the respondent company for a period of 8 hours and their wages were fixed at Rs. 1,000 per day. The respondent company was directed to pay the said amount as remuneration for overtime work. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that section 13 fixes the number of hours of work in a normal working day and this number is inclusive of one and more specified interval. The High Court held that the appellants were entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond 12 hours. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The provisions of r. 25(1) are not applicable to the case because the total number of working days in a week is 48 (8 hours per day for 6 days). [41C] (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a regular working day is achieved by pres cribing that the hours of working in a six day week shall not spread over more than ten and a half hours in any day. It will also be noticed that the scheme of section 13 fixed the number for rest shall not exceed 48, though on any particular day the hours are of work and the total period of work is part of the normal working days which may also include one or several specified intervals of rest. [41D E] (iii) The workers at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks worked in a different way and their case cannot be compared with that of the Flotilla Crew or the crew at the Alexandra Docks. The crew at that time get a specified interval of one hour for rest and this is achieved only by prescribing the hours for rest. The workers are therefore entitled to 3 hours ' wages if required, to work upto 9 hours on any day and work up to 9 hours in a twelvehour shift. [42E F] (iv) The crew in the instant case had not been able to break up the hours by interposing intervals for rest in that manner on any other day. They point out that in the former there is 3 hours of overtime and in the latter there is 4 hours of time in the 12 hour shift, but at the Principal 's & Victoria Dock and due.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in which accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976. The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had let out the premises to the appellant for the second time and that the accommodation was not required for his own use as he had no other suitable accommodation. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to protection of Section 20(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since during the pendency of the proceedings in the court 10 years have elapsed and therefore the appellant tenant will be entitled to the benefit of the provisions of Section 40 of the Rent Act, the appellant tenancy would be governed by the provisions contained in Section 20 clause (2) Sec. 2(2). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether the provisions are applicable or not is a mixed question of law and fact. [167D] 2.1 In order to attract section 39, the suit must be pending on the date of commencement of the Delhi Rent Control Act and this is the view taken in Om Prakash Gupta 's case. It is well settled that if during the period of 10 years the tenant has been entitled to a protection under the Act and in coming to this conclusion the Court also considered the language of Section 39 which is applicable to the present case. [168E] 2(a) The appellant tenant would be entitled only to the protection under section 20 clause(2), as provided for in clause (1) quoted above. It will be the date on which the first assessment was made and so far as this question is concerned, it will not apply to the suit. [169F] 2b) In order that a decree may be passed in favour of the tenant, he must be in possession of the premises for the last 10 years. If within the language Of section 39 the appellant is entitled to any benefit of section 20(1), he would be entitle to the advantage of the Section even if the matter is pending in this Court and 10 years had elapsed since then.

The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment of the appellant on the ground that he was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3 of the Act. The trial court held that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been in possession of the premises and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case for fresh disposal on merits. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that: (i) section 4 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 as amended by the Act of 1953 did not apply to a case where the appellant was a thika tenant within the meaning of the said Act as it was finally amended; and (ii) that section 4 being prospective only, it could not apply in the instant case. HELD: (1) The provisions of the Bengal Thika tenancy Act 1949 were applicable to all suits and proceedings pending on 21st October before any court or Controller within the definition of the word 'hect ' in section 2(2) of the West Bengal Thiaka Tenancy Act 1949, as amended in 1953. [710 D] (a) The words "in accordance with the provisions of this Act" in section 4 are wide enough to include all suits, appeals and proceedings instituted before any Court or Controller under the Act, but they do not mean that they must be taken into account for purposes of determining whether a person is a thikka tenant within that meaning. [810 D E] (b) The word 'may ' in the context of section 4(2), as it stood prior to 1953, was intended to include cases where the landlord wanted to eject a thata tenant after the Act had come into force and the Controller had to deal with all pre Acts suits on the basis that no notice under section 4 was necessary. [910 D F] (c) The expression "in conformity with any other law for the time being in force" in s.4(2)(a) of this section means that the provisions contained in the Act are not inconsistent with the other laws for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions thereof. [1020 G H] (d) Section 4(1) of Act, 1953, as it stands at present, is prospective only and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to establish the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 in order to succeed. [1121 D E; 1122 A B] (e) The proviso to s.3(2A) of that Act provides that where a landlord wishes to eject any thika tenants after the commencement of this Ordinance, he has to consider whether any of the ground specified in s 4 is available to him and if so, he did not have to file a suit but apply to the controller for an order in that behalf.

The High Court of Allahabad, Bench Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. The High Court directed that all Bench Secretaries irrespective of their grades should be given the pay scale admissible to Section Officers and their quality of work may vary. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the High Court had completely overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules framed by the Chief Justice for promotion to Bench Secretary Grade I, there could not be two scales of pay in the same cadre for persons having same duties and responsibilities. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to be construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of Pay and other conditions of service. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge with fixing the pay scales have to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is shown that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [292B C] 2. The principles of " equal pay for Equal work" have to he construed in a different context. One can deny that normally the difference between the two posts with different pay scales in the cadre of persons performing the same or similar work is violative of the right to have equal pay. [293C D] 3. It is against this background that the principle of 'equal pay ' has to he interpreted in the second place. The classification made under the rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [294E F] 4. The Court Secretaries Grade I are in a higher scale than Bench Secretaries Grade II. It may be that the difference was a matter which is of degree but there is no element of valuation by thosewho are charged for fixing the Pay scales. If the difference arises from an element or factor of value, it would not be interfered by the court unless it was shown that the either it was irrational or founded on no evidence. [295E F; 296A] 5. The question is whether there could be two scale of pay for persons performing similar work or duties. If a difference arises between an element and a factor of valuation, then the same will be evaluated by a competent authority. The court cannot interfere with the Court 's order unless it has been shown that any one of them is irrational. [296F] 6. It would not affect the Bench Secretaries to get that pay scale again with effect from January 1, 1986. [298H; 296B] 7.

The appellant State of Madhya Pradesh was constituted under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. The State Government issued a notification dated April 1, 1976 under section 127A of the Municipalities Act, 1973, declaring that the area in question was declared as an industry under the M.P. Municipalities Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that respondent 1 was incompetent to exercise the powers of the Municipality or the Municipal Corporation under section 126A of Municipalities Act or section 135 of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1957, as these Acts stood on 12 February 27, 1976 when clause (d) was inserted in its present form in section 69(d). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power conferred by the State legislature on Special Area Development Authority to impose property tax on lands and buildings is not in conflict with the power conferred under the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act on the Union Government to regulate and develop the coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources. [512C] 2.1 The power of the State Legislatures under Entry 24 List II, is plenary and subject to the limitations imposed by the Constitution. It is not open to the Legislature to impose a tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the Act, respectively. The powers conferred on the State Government by section 127 A are therefore not in consonance with the provisions of the Acts. [506D] 2(a) The power under Entry 52 List I is plenary in nature and subject only to the limitation imposed by Parliament. It cannot be said that the Legislature has no competence or authority to pass a law on the subject. [504E F] (b) The State Legislature has not competence to impose tax without complying with the procedure laid down by sections 128 and 133, respectively of the Indian Penal Code or the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue Act, 1961. [412F G] 2.(a) It is well settled that the power of taxation under Entry 54 List I of the Seventh Schedule is subject to two conditions namely (i) that there must be a tax on land and buildings; (ii) that it must be in respect of "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union, and (iii) that the property tax shall not be leviable, inter alia, on "buinery and lands". [506F G]. (b). The power to impose the property taxes is a legislative power. It can be exercised only if it is shown that the tax has been collected by the owner of the land or building or any other person. [ 506G] 2:2. The expression "buaces and lands" in Entry 52 of List I, is not defined in the Constitution as meaning "land". The word "build" is used in the sense of a right to hold property. It includes all rights which are capable of being exercised by the owners of land or buildings. [312A B] 3:2 The power given to the State under Entry 23, List III, is subject onlyto the limitations prescribed by the Acts mentioned therein. The legislative power conferred on Special Areas Development Authority by section 126(1) is not subject to any limitation imposed in the Act of 1957 made by Parliament and that the ownership rights could be validly acquired by the Government under the State Act. [323F G; 323A B]. 3:3.

The appellant was a lessee of a land in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government. The appellant filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that the lease was granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease had been terminated by the Government under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, the appellant could not be evicted from the land in question. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to continue in possession of land on July 1. The High Court held that the termination of the lease by the State was illegal and void as against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the words "such rights" in the third proviso have reference to the rights created after July 1,. 1945, but after July I, 1945 for a further period exceeding two years would not be enforceable against Government; (ii) the third Proviso has reference to rights created before the notified date but after August 1, 1946, for a certain period. The words " such right" in section 20 (1) are wide enough to include all rights created prior to July I 1945, which have been expressly declared by the second provisos to section 19(2); and (iii) the word "such right" has reference only to those rights created during the period of one year.
